author: AfricanFeminism
title: Morocco’s First Woman Prime Minister and the Terms of Freedom
content:
Something changes when a woman occupies an office men have treated as their natural inheritance. Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri’s

appointment

 on 29 September 2026 makes that change visible in Morocco. For women whose competence is routinely scrutinised, the pleasure is neither naïve nor trivial.


But the woman forming a government and the woman labouring in the fields, raising children without pay and denied an equal share of her inheritance encounter power differently. Representation changes who governs; emancipation changes what all women have the power to do. That distinction shifts our attention from PM Mansouri’s gender to the politics of the centre-right

 Party of Authenticity and Modernity (PAM

)

, which she leads. Will its programme redistribute the resources and rights on which women’s freedom depends?


The history beneath the headline


Calling women’s leadership foreign to Morocco requires forgetting its history. Historian Osire Glacier

documents

 women’s authority long before the contemporary premiership. Kenza al Awrabiya, the Amazigh mother of Idris II, helped secure the Idrisid dynasty, founded in the late eighth century in what is now Morocco. Zaynab al Nafzawiyya influenced eleventh-century Almoravid politics around Aghmat, near Marrakech. Sayyida al Hurra governed Tétouan, a city in northern Morocco, during the sixteenth century. Khnata bint Bakkar intervened in eighteenth-century dynastic politics.


Across the region,

Dihya

 is remembered as an Amazigh queen who led resistance to the Arab conquest in the Aurès, in present-day Algeria, during the late seventh century. Tuareg oral tradition remembers

Tin Hinan

 as a queen and founding ancestress of noble lineages in the Ahaggar, in present-day southern Algeria.


These histories expose how male authority is made to appear natural. Fatima Mernissi’s

The Forgotten Queens of Islam


challenges that selective memory. Colonialism also reorganised authority: French Protectorate administrators

reshaped

 customary courts around imperial priorities. What survives as tradition can carry the history of political intervention. 


Religious interpretation can give exclusion another claim to permanence. Islamist and other conservative opponents invoke this

hadith

 against women’s political authority:


«لَنْ يُفْلِحَ قَوْمٌ وَلَّوْا أَمْرَهُمُ امْرَأَةً»


Usually translated as saying that a people governed by a woman will not prosper, it becomes a prohibition irrespective of her competence. Asma Lamrabet, a

Moroccan Islamic feminist thinker

, questions turning a

narration linked

 to Persia’s dynastic succession into a universal ban. She reads it against the Qur’anic Queen of Sheba, whose judgement demonstrates capable leadership. Her argument contests male authority’s claim to divine necessity.


PAM’s promises and its record


Women have long contested how authority is distributed within the family. Fatima Sadiqi

documents

the Union de l’Action Féminine’s 1992 million-signature campaign to reform the Moudawana, Morocco’s family code. The 2004 reform abolished wives’ duty of obedience but retained unequal inheritance and exceptions to the marriage age of eighteen. Proposals announced in December 2024 left fundamental equality demands unresolved. In October 2025, more than sixty civil society organisations and public figures

joined to call for comprehensive reform

. Rights in Morocco have advanced through organised demands, not the gender of an officeholder.


PAM, a centre-right party founded in 2008,

advocates

 social modernisation and positions itself against the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD). It entered government in 2021 alongside the National Rally of Independents and conservative nationalist Istiqlal. Opposition to Islamist conservatism, however, does not itself entail reforming the laws and economic conditions that subordinate women.


PAM’s

2026 programme

 promises improved widow pensions, childcare, safe transport, a women’s enterprise fund and labour inspection. The commitments leave inheritance equality, abortion reform and decriminalisation of consensual same sex relations unaddressed. Mansouri called for

banning child marriage

 without exceptions in 2024, yet PAM’s electoral programme

omits that commitment

. Employment can support independence, but a wage does not cancel criminalisation or unequal property rights. The programme leaves those constraints intact.


Even PAM’s narrow promise to increase …

author: WoMin
title: Press Release | Women’s Climate Assembly strengthens Pan African solidarity, women-led resistance and the struggle for a just future
content:
“

Empowering women is a radical way to transform the world!

” –

Ivorian activist


The fourth regional

Women’s Climate Assembly

 (WCA), held in Yaoundé, Cameroon, from 5–8 October 2026, concluded with a powerful reaffirmation of African women’s determination to defend their lands, territories, livelihoods and communities, and to demand climate justice and reparations.


Under the theme, “

Our lands, our voices: African women united for climate justice and reparations!

”, the Assembly convened over 75 women community leaders, activists, feminist organisations, civil society groups and allies from twelve countries including Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Guinea-Conakry, Liberia, Namibia, Niger, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Senegal and Zambia.


The gathering provided a vital space for women on the frontlines of the climate crisis, extractive industries, land dispossession and environmental destruction to share their experiences, strengthen relationships across borders and build collective strategies for change.


As the Assembly closed, one message rang clear: African women are not merely bearing the costs of the climate crisis. They are leading the struggle for solutions, defending their communities and shaping the future they want.


“

There’s an adage in my village that women cannot build a nation. The Women’s Climate Assembly has proved that women build nations. We counter this adage with the unity and solidarity of African women!”

 –

DRC activist-participant


Turning shared struggles into collective power


From communities confronting oil and gas expansion and destructive mining to women defending forests, seeds, water sources and ancestral lands, participants brought forward the lived realities of communities too often excluded from decisions about their territories and futures.


Through collective reflection, popular education and movement-building, women connected struggles that may take place in different countries but are rooted in common systems of exploitation, inequality and environmental destruction.


Designed by women activists and members of the WCA Steering Committee, the thematic teach-ins explored a range of political concepts, questions and practices, including:


The erosion of farmers’ seeds

: A challenge for building resilient and sustainable food systems. What solutions are there for preserving our seed heritage?  


Nature Commons

: The defence of the Congo Basin’s forests.


Counting the Costs of Mal/Bad Development and Demanding reparations

: The case of the African Development Bank campaign.


Fighting some of the false solutions to the climate crisis

: Gas extraction, enclosure of our forests and lands for carbon trading, green conservation and more.


Building democratic, accountable, ‘loving’ leadership

: Why are these principles so important to feminist leadership? What else do we feel is critical to leading as feminists?


Lessons on organising and movement building

: Growing National/sub-regional grassroots movements.


Building knowledge from what we know

: Building feminist popular knowledge as the basis for Building Women’s Power. How can we go about doing this locally in our communities and beyond that.


The WCA celebrated the knowledge, resistance and organising power of rural, Indigenous, peasant and working-class women. The

Each One, Teach One

 sessions embodied this spirit of knowledge-sharing, collective learning and liberation. On Day Two, participants exchanged practical skills, crafts and tools, sharing techniques for making baobab candies, producing eco-briquettes from cassava and creating seed bricks to cultivate and protect Indigenous seeds. Weaving, cloth-dyeing, beadwork and other practices also featured, affirming the value of knowledge held, practised and passed down through generations of women.


The gathering reaffirmed the importance of strengthening a Pan African ecofeminist movement that recognises the connections between the climate crisis, extractivism, gender injustice, food insecurity and the loss of community control over natural resources.


It also reinforced a fundamental principle: communities must have the power to determine their own futures, including the right to say NO to destructive development projects that threaten their lands, livelihoods and ways of life.


Climate justice means reparations, not empty promises

author: Caleb Okereke
title: Matthew Blaise wants to be your friend and neighbor
content:
Matthew Blaise and I must have been in our mid teens when we first met. I don’t remember the exact year, but I remember that it was on Facebook. It did not take long for that online connection to become a real friendship, and it is one that has persisted despite life carrying us in different directions.   


When we sit down for this conversation in September, I am in Philadelphia and Matthew is in Brazil. He is preparing for

Friends and Neighbors

, a new art and literary festival in Lagos built around a deceptively simple question: What responsibility do we have to the people we call our friends and our neighbors?


It is a question that makes our own friendship an interesting place from which to begin. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 


Caleb:

 Something I find provocative about the title “Friends and Neighbors” is that you also seem to be making a statement about the ways queerness shows up in the ordinary. I’m thinking about this song, “Your driver could be LGBT, your friend could be LGBT, your neighbour could be LGBT.” Was that part of the conceptual framing?


Matthew:

 Actually, that’s another way to see it. When I thought of this concept, I thought of proximity within our community. A trip from Lagos to Europe is cheaper than a trip from Lagos to Abidjan, which is a neighboring country. For me, that’s a metaphor for what a lot of friendship within the African continent, especially around queerness, has been due to bad policy, homophobia and criminalization.


Queer people within Africa are not so familiar with themselves. And in that sense, we really haven’t constructed what queer Africanness is because we are still not so close to ourselves. But I find it interesting that you also see it from the point of everyday life, where people you come in contact with could be of this community or could possess these identities without you knowing.


Caleb:

 That’s what immediately came to my attention. Even when you say, “Hello, friends. Hello, neighbors,” you’re talking to all of us, right? It’s not “queer friends and neighbors.” The implicit read is that even if you’re straight, queer people are all around you. They’re your friends. They’re your neighbors. They might not tell you that they’re queer, but they’re there.


Matthew:

 From the perspective of bell hooks, societies should be built on love and friendship. This very important foundation of love has been taken away from queer people, or we’ve not been given that due to our queerness. Governmental policies and criminalization also make us live our lives in isolation. What it means to be friends right now is also very transactional, especially for queer people.


Caleb:

 One thing that has defined our friendship, at least for me, is honesty. There are things I can tell you that I can’t tell anybody else, obviously, so a sort of radical honesty. And as you were talking about transactional relationships, it made me think, what is the place of honesty in friendship, especially in a context where being honest about yourself can carry consequences?


Matthew:

 I think you don’t owe everyone that truth about yourself. For those who I truly trust, I owe them that responsibility of truth. And I do believe, for every friendship, there has to be that investment in honesty.


Caleb:

 But friendship in and of itself is a risk. I don’t think we realize that, but every friendship is a risk.


Matthew:

 Yeah, friendship sometimes, I mean, it’s not a constant state of feeling a certain way. It’s a roller coaster of emotions. It’s a journey. It’s an adventure. So you encounter a lot of things on the way.


You stretch your hand to someone and they actually bite your hand, then you know they are not really having that good intention towards you. So you can decide to stretch your hand again or push them away. But for me, I think it’s important that we’re able to stretch our hands and bring people together and do the work of educating them until we just know they’re irredeemable.


Caleb:

 Yeah…


Matthew:

 What responsibility do you think you owe me as your friend?


Caleb:

 You are now the one asking me questions. But no, I mean, I think you owe your friend loyalty. That’s one of the things that I’m non-negotiable on. I mean, there are many other things you owe your friend.


Matthew:

 You owe them honesty also?


Caleb:

 You owe them honesty. You also owe your friends grace. I give grace a lot. Maybe it’s not even grace. I’m also like, oh …

author: Amadou Diarra
title: Wood for War: How Wagner Was Paid in Central African Forest
content:
On 9 February 2021, as government troops and Russian mercenaries pushed rebels back from Bangui, the Central African Republic (CAR) signed Decree No. 21.044. It gave a young company called Bois Rouge a forestry permit covering 186,596 hectares in the south-western Lobaye region –

roughly 1,866 km² of tropical forest, an area larger than Greater London

.


Bois Rouge had never logged a tree. What it had, according to the

US Treasury

, was a patron: the concession was granted in exchange for services the Wagner Group provided to the CAR, at about the same time Wagner fighters and government forces were recapturing territory from the rebels.


Pieced together from sanctions files, customs data and transparency reports, the story shows how Wagner turned battlefield gains into commodities – and why timber proved a poor currency for a sanctioned militia.


A Russian Company with a Central African Face


Flag of the Central African Republic


Bois Rouge SARLU was

registered in Bangui in March 2019

. On paper it was a local firm with a Central African boss.

By October 2019

, at a forestry forum in Shanghai, Bois Rouge was listed under ‘Russia’, represented by Russians Artem Tolmachov and ‘Mike’ Vdovin.


A

UK parliamentary inquiry into the Wagner network

 later named Tolmachov as Bois Rouge’s commercial director. The research group All Eyes on Wagner

found he was also paid

 by two other companies tied to Wagner founder Yevgeny Prigozhin: Service K, which also financed the diamond firm Diamville, and Ferrum Mining, active in Madagascar. The pattern is familiar: a local shell in front, Russian managers behind.


The paperwork moved fast. The

CAR’s 2021 report to the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (EITI)

 and a

forestry sector review

 record the permit, PEA 193, with 137,585 exploitable hectares and a management plan approved on 28 April 2021 – less than three months after the decree. The terms were generous: the newcomer received a moratorium on concession rent and export tax, which researchers consider unlawful and which cost the state and communities revenue.


The company built its sawmill in Boda, a town

government forces and Wagner had cleared of rebels

 shortly before the permit was issued. This sets the case apart from ordinary illegal logging. The wood was not smuggled out of a lawless forest. It was licensed by the state, as payment for war.


From Boda to Douala


The export route, as reconstructed by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), ran from Boda to the ‘Kassaï’ military base in Bangui, then by road through Cameroon to the port of Douala. A GI-TOC photograph from 7 June 2023 shows a loaded company truck at Kassaï. That logs were staged at a military base says much about who ran the business.


The Treasury lists the species exported: azobé, iroko, mukulungu, tali and, above all, sapele. Supplies flowed the other way through Broker Expert, a St Petersburg firm long used by Prigozhin, which made dozens of deliveries for Bois Rouge and, according to the Treasury, also moved the network’s money. Trade data showed

hundreds of imports

 of Russian machinery and logging equipment.


Most timber went to Turkey, the UAE and China, but some reached Europe.

Earthsight found

 that in 2022 the Danish firm WoodGroup ApS, a subsidiary of London-based Woodbois, took six shipments – 465 m³ of sapele worth an estimated €3.4 million at retail. One shipment was recorded as going to France’s Tropica-Bois, whose manager

told Earthsight

 the company had never bought the wood – a discrepancy, not proof of complicity.


New Names, Same Wood


After All Eyes on Wagner began publishing in 2022, Bois Rouge became Wood International Group (WIG) and

hired a new Central African director and a new Russian commercial director

. It did not help. In 2023,

CBS News filmed

 timber convoys heading from a Wagner-linked base to Cameroon and obtained about 100 WIG export documents whose details matched those of Bois Rouge.


OFAC, the Treasury’s sanctions office,

designated the company in September 2023

. In March 2024 the Treasury detailed its Wagner ties and sanctioned Broker Expert, after a joint probe with

Homeland Security Investigations

. Britain followed on 13 June 2024 (

UK sanctions list

; notices in the

Isle of Man

 and

Guernsey

). In Douala, WIG cargo was already being held up in June 2023.


GI-TOC counts 839 m³ exported in 2022 and a peak of 5,810 m³ …

author: Gary Chartier
title: Propedeutica al Libertarismo di Sinistra
content:
Di

Gary Chartier

. Originale:

Framing Left Libertarianism: A First Pass

, del 25 ottobre 2012. Tradotto da

Enrico Sanna

.


Questo articolo, scritto da

Gary Chartier

, è stato pubblicato originariamente sul suo blog

Liberalaw

 

il dieci dicembre 2008

.


Qualcuno considera il libertarismo di sinistra un esercizio cosmetico e propagandistico. Ma c’è anche chi ci vede l’espressione forte di questioni che dovrebbero stare al centro dei movimenti per la libertà.


Ci sono cinici libertari e persone di sinistra che nel libertarismo di sinistra vedono una falsa propaganda politica. Nel tentativo, forse, di spacciare a ignare persone di sinistra ideali libertari in contrasto con il programma della sinistra. O forse è il tentativo di infondere un’anima aliena nel corpo del movimento libertario, gravandolo di questioni inesistenti in un vero programma libertario.


Nessuna di queste ipotesi è anche lontanamente persuasiva o interessante.


Il libertarismo di sinistra è profondamente libertario perché è antistatalista (i primi libertari di sinistra che mi vengono in mente sono tutti anarchici: do per scontato che sono tutti anarchici o pressoché tali) e perché conferma il valore del mercato e dei diritti di proprietà. Ma è anche di sinistra perché lotta contro il privilegio, il potere gerarchico, l’esclusione, la privazione e il dominio sia ideologicamente che praticamente, e perché dimostra un sincero attaccamento ai concetti di inclusione, emancipazione e rispetto reciproco.


E lo fa non ridefinendo i termini, così che, ad esempio, la libertà si riduce alla libertà dalla costrizione fisica, ma evidenziando la sintonia tra ideali e principi libertari e concetti di fondo di sinistra.


Ovvero illustrando le conseguenze radicali di un’adesione ai principi libertari.


• Si capirebbe allora che la legittimità della proprietà è viziata da tutta una storia di violenze, collusioni o aiuti da parte dello stato a persone e organizzazioni ricche e potenti, fatto che giustifica l’

appropriazione della loro presunta proprietà da parte di chi ci vive e lavora

.


• Davanti alle ingiustizie e alla sfacciataggine dei monopoli e degli aiuti di stato, l’adozione piena dei principi libertari minerebbe in vari modi il potere delle imprese centralizzate piramidali, facilitandone la sostituzione con cooperative di lavoratori e rafforzando enormemente il potere dei lavoratori.


• Si capirebbe così che i principi libertari portano al rifiuto di quel genere di privilegi che permettono a influenti attività d’affari, professionisti e singoli associati di servirsi del potere statale per sfruttare gli altri (come le società clientelari che ottengono privilegi fiscali sulla concorrenza, o come quelle attività corporative ricche e privilegiate che danneggiano la popolazione e la potenziale concorrenza grazie a licenze e requisiti restrittivi imposti dallo stato).


• Con l’adesione ai principi libertari, infine, diventerebbe evidente che un principio che va contro lo stato offre anche una base forte contro la guerra e soprattutto l’imperialismo.


Gli stessi principi morali che spingono a lottare contro il potere oppressivo dello stato possono offrire una buona ragione per lottare contro tutti quei poteri oppressivi che giustamente attirano l’attenzione della sinistra. Dai principi morali che guidano la lotta contro lo stato possono scaturire le questioni più diverse. Diritto naturale, teoria della virtù, kantismo, pluralismo etico, ma anche (anche se per varie ragioni mi sembra fuori luogo) consequenzialismo: tutto può fare da base dell’anarchismo di mercato o di altre questioni morali. Le ragioni che (ad esempio) nel nome dell’uguaglianza negano il “diritto naturale di governare” e l’insensibilità verso le particolarità individuali, rendono moralmente inammissibile anche il razzismo, il sessismo e l’eterosessismo.


I libertari di destra tendenzialmente rifiutano gli ideali dei libertari di sinistra per ragioni varie. Dicono (I) che non c’è niente di particolarmente libertario in questioni riguardanti il potere sul posto di lavoro o il benessere dei lavoratori, o anche il razzismo. A volte arrivano anche a dire (II) che sono questioni anti-libertarie.


Se la prima obiezione è convincente dipende in parte da come viene concepita la lotta contro il potere dello stato. Finché si basa su un certo principio morale, però, sulla base dello stesso principio si possono dare anche giudizi morali riguardanti questioni diverse dal potere dello …

author: Sara Connors
title: Yukon, Canada, ask for dismissal of $150M mining lawsuit launched by First Nation of Na-Cho Nyäk Dun
content:
The Yukon and federal governments are refuting a $150 million lawsuit launched last year by a First Nation alleging they were negligent in a mining disaster and failed to uphold its treaty rights.


The First Nation of

Na-Cho Nyäk Dun

 (FNNND), located approximately a five-hour drive north of Whitehorse,

filed the lawsuit against the territorial and federal governments last December.


Part of the lawsuit targets the territorial government and its handling of the heap-leach failure at the Eagle mine site in June 2024. The incident saw about two million tonnes of cyanide-soaked ore escape containment, releasing cyanide-containing solution into the surrounding environment on the First Nation’s traditional territory.


After what Yukon admitted was a “catastrophic failure,” the First Nation

made ardent calls for a public inquiry into the incident

—calls that went unanswered.


Former chief Dawna Hope told APTN News at the time that the First Nation was frustrated by what she characterized as a lack of government accountability since the disaster took place, and that, as a signatory to its final agreement, it has a duty to co-manage the First Nation’s lands and resources.


The lawsuit also accuses the government of dragging its feet in developing a land use plan for nearly half of the First Nation’s traditional territory, which it argues further violates its treaty rights.


It asks for a temporary ban on new mineral staking on its territory until either a land use plan is completed, mutually acceptable interim protections are put in place or the lawsuit reaches a conclusion.


But Yukon’s statement of defence, filed on Oct. 7, disputes the bulk of the First Nation’s claims.


That includes its argument that the Eagle mine incident was appropriately managed. It states that the project proceeded through the proper procedural and regulatory channels before production started, and that after the incident, it acted accordingly.


That includes seeking and obtaining receivership for the mine site, providing the necessary funding for the receivership to proceed, and throwing its weight behind an independent review board tasked with investigating the causes behind the disaster and making recommendations for improvements going forward.


The defence notes that 52 of 56 of the board’s recommendations are completed while the other four are underway, with all recommendations expected to be completed around next spring.


“Yukon met its legal obligations to regulate, monitor, inspect, enforce, investigate, respond to, remediate, or otherwise manage matters relating to the Eagle Gold Mine,” it states. “None of Yukon’s acts or omissions caused, contributed to, or failed to prevent the Eagle Gold Mine Incident.”


The defence also points a finger back at the First Nation over land use planning, accusing it of hindering progress.


It claims that the First Nation “often refused” the government’s invitations to engage. It states that the First Nation required “preconditions” in participating in proposed land use planning, resulting in “ultimatums, including requests for staking moratoria over 100% of FNNND Traditional Territory.”


The defence notes that both parties

entered into an MOU last year to start the land use planning process

, something it says is still in effect.


“Yukon is committed to meaningful and good faith participation in the land use planning process, and will continue to consult and engage with FNNND in good faith and in a manner consistent with the provisions of the Final Agreement, the Honour of the Crown and the terms of the MOU,” it states.


It goes on to say that FNNND has likewise shunted the territory’s work on draft minerals legislation, which would give First Nations more say over mining projects on their traditional territories.


The First Nation

publicly panned the proposed framework last summer

, accusing it of not going far enough to implement the sweeping changes it argues are needed to overhaul the territory’s minerals legislation.


But the defence alleges that despite providing the First Nation with funding to build capacity to work on the framework, it made numerous demands, including a veto over all mining activity on its traditional territory and requiring staking to be withdrawn from its entire traditional territory before advancing successor legislation.


The defence says that while other First Nations parties agreed to the proposed draft framework in March 2025, FNNND “declined to …

author: Arezu Fayyazi
title: Domestic Violence and Femicide in Afghanistan: Women Are Denied Protection and Justice
content:
Domestic violence has intensified under Taliban rule since August 2021, as the regime has imposed more than 160 edicts and directives restricting the rights and freedoms of women and girls. By barring women from education and employment, severely limiting their freedom of movement, and denying them meaningful access to justice, the Taliban has deepened women’s dependence on their families and left many with fewer ways to escape abuse or seek protection. In this climate of systemic oppression and impunity, domestic violence can go unchallenged, while women and girls face the devastating risk of femicide.

Reports from The Guardian and Zan Times have recorded 231 cases of femicide across just ten provinces -there are 34 provinces – in Afghanistan since 2021. However, it is important to note that these reports emphasized the fact that these cases of femicide do not represent all of the cases in the country since 2021, given the fact that it’s difficult to record these instances of domestic violence after the Taliban has removed avenues to report these crimes.

The Taliban has dismantled the Ministry of Women’s Affairs, the prosecutor’s office that handled violence against women, and women’s shelters all together. Additionally, women judges and men judges that were trained on domestic violence issues and supported women, have all been removed. With the Taliban’s return to power, roughly 250 female judges lost their jobs and were banned from practicing. All those positions were filled with Taliban members, most of whom have no official training in law. The complete dismantling of all legal protections for women in Afghanistan has contributed to the increased rates of domestic violence in addition to a lack of legal accountability for men who commit domestic violence.

Even worse, the victims of just the recorded cases ranged from 5 to 65. Of these 231 cases, only 58 cases resulted in arrests of the suspect committing violence, only roughly 25% of cases. The lack of accountability for domestic violence is reinforced by the Taliban’s astonishing new Criminal Procedure Regulation of the Courts released in February 2026. In these regulations, it “allows husbands to physically punish their wives as long as the violence does not result in ‘broken bones or serious visible injuries.’” This regulation is evidence of the Taliban’s disregard for the rights, safety, and wellbeing of women. This new regulation just allows domestic violence to occur with no repercussions, and women are left paying the consequences with their dignity and lives. Liza Shams, a victim of domestic violence, passed away after going to the hospital for “being severely beaten” with “multiple fractures to her facial bones.”

The systematic oppression of women has left a huge burden on Afghan women not just physically, but also mentally and emotionally. With the lack of support or possibility to leave a relationship of domestic violence, there has been an increase in suicide due to psychological pressure. According to data from the UN, 7 in 10 women “describe their mental health as ‘bad’ or ‘very bad.’” Hasina, a young woman who was just 22 years old, took her own life after experiencing domestic violence from her husband and his family. Her uncle spoke out and said her death was “a killing caused by violence and oppression, even if the final act was carried out by her own hand.” He goes on to say “at such a young age, she had already gone through so much. She should have been studying, growing and preparing for a brighter future. Instead, she found herself in circumstances where, from her perspective, ending her life appeared to be the only escape.”

There is enough evidence to demonstrate that domestic violence is not just a household issue, but one compounded by a political system that strips women of their autonomy, protections, and opportunities. When women are banned from going to school, earning an income, seeking justice, or becoming independent – escaping an abusive situation is incredibly difficult. The consequences leave women isolated, psychologically distressed, and in the most tragic cases – dead.

Afghan women have repeatedly made clear that they deserve more than expressions of international concern. Their suffering must not remain hidden behind the closed doors of abusive households and be further obscured by the Taliban’s systematic efforts to erase women from public life and silence their voices. Without access to legal protection, education …

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Casual student support staff approvals in Nunavut drops from 75 to 15
content:
Nunavut’s Education Department approved 15 requests for casual student support assistants this school year, one-fifth of the number it approved the school year prior.


Of those 15, a total of 11 have been hired, according to figures the department provided Nunatsiaq News Wednesday.


The department is recruiting workers for the remaining four positions, spokesperson Kuthula Matshazi said in an email.


He said some positions couldn’t get filled despite recruiting efforts. Others remained vacant due to relief employees filling in or workers going on leave.


Student support workers join classroom teachers to help them deliver the curriculum. They work with individual students who require accommodations and those who follow unique education guidelines. School leaders can submit requests for casual support staff when they don’t have enough permanent staff to meet demand.


There is currently 206.5 support positions allocated to the territory, Matshazi said, 161 of which are being filled indeterminately. The department has also hired 164 on-call relief employees this year, to fill in for support workers who are on leave.


In the 2025-26 school year, the department approved 75 requests for casual support staff, resulting in 36 hires.


There are fewer casual support staff

assigned

 to Nunavut’s classrooms this year after Inuit Child First Initiative policies changed in February 2025.


That’s when Indigenous Services Canada disqualified funding requests through the initiative for student support assistants. Requests can still be submitted, but they are now considered on a case-by-case basis and approved only in exceptional circumstances.


During the 2024-25 school year, the funding program allowed district education authorities to hire 88 casual student support assistants, adding an extra number to those the Government of Nunavut regularly employs.

author: Chris Walker
title: Supreme Court Rejects Trump Bid to Halt Care for Incarcerated Trans People
content:
The decision is a rare win for transgender rights at the conservative-leaning Supreme Court.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The U.S. Supreme Court has denied an emergency petition from the Trump administration, which sought a stay on a lower court’s injunction on a policy that would have denied gender-affirming care to federally incarcerated transgender people.

That policy was implemented by the Bureau of Prisons (BOP) after President Donald Trump signed an executive order in January 2025 that denied the existence of transgender people. The order also directed federal agencies to take steps that would be consistent with that view, and included specific instructions for the BOP.

“The Attorney General shall ensure that the Bureau of Prisons revises its policies concerning medical care to be consistent with this order, and shall ensure that no Federal funds are expended for any medical procedure, treatment, or drug for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex,” the order reads.

After the BOP conformed to the order, a group of incarcerated trans people who had been receiving gender-affirming care sued the administration. The group is being represented by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), which argued that their Eighth Amendment protections against cruel and unusual punishment were being infringed upon.

A federal judge agreed, and, in August, ordered the policy to be blocked. The Trump administration challenged that finding, but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit upheld it, prompting Solicitor General John Sauer to submit an emergency appeal to the Supreme Court.

The court has regularly ruled against transgender people, allowing state bans on trans athletes’ participation in sports, ruling in favor of a ban on transgender people in the military, and upholding state laws that bar gender-affirming care for trans children and teens. Yet on Wednesday, the court denied the Trump administration’s request.

“The application for stay presented to The Chief Justice and by him referred to the Court is denied,” the order read, giving no further explanation. Two justices for the court — Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas — would have granted the Trump administration’s request for a stay, the document said.

The ACLU heralded the high court’s denial of the emergency petition, stating, “This ruling affirms that federal prison officials can’t deny transgender people essential health care.”

Around 1,000 federally incarcerated trans people have also been diagnosed with gender dysphoria. The ruling means these individuals can continue receiving gender-affirming care while they remain in federal prisons or jails and the case moves forward in the lower courts.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Khushi Arora, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Williams Lake First Nation memorializes history and justice with opening of Sḱulé7ten Park
content:
Williams Lake First Nation Willie Sellars speaks about the significance of Sḱulé7ten park during its official opening.

Photo by Khushi Arora


This story was originally printed in the

Williams Lake Tribune

 and appears here with minor style edits.


The Williams Lake First Nation (WLFN) celebrated the grand opening of a new memorial park in downtown Williams Lake, unveiling its name as Sḱulé7ten Park.


WLFN, also known as T’exelc, welcomed the community to the park on Oct. 13. The space memorializes WLFN’s journey towards reaching a historic specific claim settlement with “Canada.” The colonial government illegally displaced the First Nation from their traditional village site 165 years ago, in what’s now the City of Williams Lake.


After guiding attendees through the pronunciation of the park’s name “skoo LET nn,” WLFN member William Lulua explained that the surrounding area included spaces where people did vision quests. Although there was a disconnection from the practice as Williams Lake developed into a city, he said the names of the people received through those places could not be taken away.


William Lulua shares the history and meaning behind Sḱulé7ten park’s name during the official opening on Tuesday, Oct.13. Photo by Khushi Arora


According to the Facebook post by WLFN, the name Sḱulé7ten is the traditional Secwepemcstin word for the area that makes up downtown Williams Lake, and the name translates to “where you find yourself.”


Before the main opening drum song, Elder Virginia Gilbert was called upon to do a prayer. She spoke about attending both day and residential “schools,” expressing gratitude that her five children had not attended those institutions. She gave thanks for her ancestors, family, food, water and medicines, and asked that the park provide a place for rest for people struggling with addictions.


“Great spirit, let this place bless them and look after them,” added Gilbert.


Students from Little Chiefs Primary School performed drumming and songs during the ceremony. 


Little Chiefs Primary School students drum and sing during the official opening of Sḱulé7ten park on Tuesday, Oct.13. Photo by Khushi Arora


WLFN Chief Willie Sellars thanked the students, recognizing the strength it takes to perform and carry forward songs significant to the First Nation and their ancestors.


Sellars also thanked the contractors who helped design and build the park and said, “we couldn’t have done it without all those contractors stepping up and contributing to this project, city representatives, community members and WLFN staff who attended the opening.”


WLFN councillor and director of self-government Chris Wycotte recalled the First Nation’s persistence through decades of pursuing its specific claim.


“We just said, no, we’re going to take it as far as we can,” said Wycotte.


Community members gather to celebrate the official opening of Sḱulé7ten memorial park in downtown Williams Lake on Oct. 13. Photo by Khushi Arora


He described finding documents in the provincial archives that revealed an injustice against the First Nation. After repeated rejections, WLFN continued pursuing the claim through legal proceedings, eventually taking its fight to the Supreme Court of Canada.


“And this is what we end up with today. And this park here is just a memorial to that journey,” he added.


Chief Sellars acknowledged relationships with municipal, provincial and federal governments, saying collaboration had helped bring community to where it is today.


“And that relationship has been tough at times, but where we’re at right now, we’re in a good place,” Sellars added.


“Under the settlement, Canada provided the Williams Lake First Nation with $135 million in total compensation,” the federal government stated in a September 2023 news release about the Village Site Specific Claim.


Sellars said the First Nation’s approach to the settlement honours its ancestors while providing for future generations. He described the opening as an opportunity for the wider community to participate in reconciliation.


“That’s taking care of our generations, four, five, six, seven generations from now, and that is what we are very proud of as Williams Lake First Nation,” he continued.


WLFN manager of culture and language Cecil Sheena introduced a grass dance with Reggie Sandy and Sellars and invited drummers to take part.


Afterward, Sellars thanked Sheena and the drummers and invited another round of applause …

title: ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ Kicked Off Season 23 With a Sapphic Smooch
content:
Grey’s Anatomy came back with a bang. (Well, a smooch. But we’ll get there.) Amelia spent the entire episode getting the cold shoulder from Toni because, as I’m sure you remember, we left them last season with Toni showing up at Amelia’s door to profess her love for her, only to realize a naked Cass was already in Amelia’s apartment.

When we return for season 23(!), Toni is giving Amelia the cold shoulder all day. Amelia desperately wants to talk to her, but Toni isn’t hearing her out. They clash over work decisions, and Amelia starts to get frustrated. And at this point I was afraid the show was ending their storyline. I thought it was going to be a dramatic fight and then back to no wlw relationships on the show. I was thankfully wrong!

Eventually, the day leads Amelia to Toni’s front door, where she apologizes again for sleeping with Cass, and explains it was an emotional reaction to being so sure Toni was about get back together with her ex. She regrets it if it means she would lose Toni. She says she’s truly, madly, deeply in love with Toni and that if Toni is done, she’ll move on, but if not, she really doesn’t want to let what they have died. Toni considers her for a moment but then breaks; she’s still in love with Amelia, and she’s not done. The two kiss about it, and while I doubt their road ahead will be paved with roses and rainbows (especially because Toni’s ex is still in the picture, and goodness knows if/when Cass will return to drop bombs) but I’m glad we at least aren’t done with their story yet. I look forward to seeing what Season 23 will bring for our resident gays; here’s hoping none of them disappear into the parking lot of no return.

author: Saima Desai
title: Beating burnout in social movements requires strategy
content:
This article

Beating burnout in social movements requires strategy

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


I recently showed up to a protest for the first time in months, looked around, and thought: “Who the hell

are

 all these people?” 


Friends I could once rely on running into at protests when I was younger were missing. 


The fact that I hadn’t been to a protest in months was unusual. I’d had a hard season of exhaustion and cynicism, and I felt I was falling out of the loop. In the last few years, I turned 30 and moved back to my hometown, and the once-intense focus on social movements that I had in my 20s was now jostling for attention with work and family. 


The absence of my comrades at that protest seemed to signal that others, too, had burned or faded out of organizing.


It’s a trend that Chris Dixon describes in his new book, which is about sticking around for the long haul in the fight for a better world: “In radical activist scenes especially,” he writes, “people tend to age out by their 30s, if not before.” 


When the manuscript of Dixon’s book came my way, it spoke to my fear of burning or fading out of the movements that have given my life meaning and momentum. (I sit on the editorial collective of Between The Lines Books, and helped select the book for publication; it was released in September 2026.) 


After a few recent boom-and-bust cycles of uprisings — 2020’s Black liberation uprising, the Palestine solidarity protests that kicked off in 2023 — it’s a timely and thoughtful book about building movements with care and commitment.


Dixon (who unfortunately shares a name with a far more famous American crypto bro) is an anti-authoritarian activist and a scholar of social movements. “For the Long Haul: How to Stay in the Fight for a Better World”

is the latest effort in his lifelong project to understand how social movements are built and sustained.


Dixon grew up in Alaska, and the book opens by describing his decades-long friendship with Ruth Sheridan, an anarchist who was in her 70s when she first came to talk to his eighth grade labor history class. That early curiosity — about how left-wing social movements are built and sustained and the unsung activists who make it happen — showed up in his 2014 book “Another Politics: Talking Across Today’s Transformative Movements,” in which he shared lessons from almost a decade spent interviewing organizers across the U.S. and Canada. 


Now, Dixon has reached back into this same conversational archive to write “For the Long Haul.” 


We meet Bill Stivers, an elder communist Dixon befriended as a teen; Rachel Herzing, the co-founder of prison abolitionist group Critical Resistance; the political prisoner David Gilbert with whom he exchanged letters from jail, and many more. 


These lifelong leftists share their observations about what leads to burnout, the many-headed monster that has long stalked social movements. During this time of totalizing neoliberalism and weakened movement infrastructure, it’s grown especially powerful. These movement veterans counsel us to be patient, open-minded and to “practice being nobody special.” 


Dixon tells the story of Stivers who, at the age of 76, travelled from Anchorage, Alaska to the state of Chiapas in southern Mexico to attend the Zapatistas’ Intercontinental Encounter for Humanity and Against Neoliberalism. It was just a couple years after the militant group’s armed uprising and a young Dixon, more swayed by a European left tradition at that time, looked on with skepticism. But Stivers ended up having the more clear-eyed assessment of this new approach to anti-capitalist struggle. Stivers had cultivated the long view, which helped him avoid cynicism and dogmatism, and encouraged him to keep learning and stay open to new developments.  


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


What I found most helpful about the book was Dixon’s formulation of burnout: he sees it not just as a type of overwork or exhaustion, but as a feeling of defeat that becomes more common because of a lack of strategy. Dixon introduces this idea by sharing a conversation he had with Kim Marks, a direct-action environmentalist and Indigenous solidarity organizer in Oregon: “So much of burnout is about not being effective,” she said, “and so much ineffectiveness comes from not having a plan.” 


Dixon traces the ways that people often burn out of activist groups back to …

author: Admin101
title: Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense
content:
Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation (BRRN) is excited to announce the publication of

Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense

.


Drawing on organizing experiences of Black Rose/Rosa Negra members across the United States, this pamphlet explores how workers, neighbors, and communities are building collective resistance to ICE and defending their immigrant coworkers, classmates, and loved ones. By connecting struggles across workplaces, schools, and neighborhoods, the

transversal organizing

 approach we prioritize builds solidarity across different sectors of society to confront the interconnected structures of domination that shape our lives.


You can find a downloadable PDF version of the pamphlet at the end of this text.


Two Years of Trump II: Immigrants in the Crosshairs, Resistance Under Attack


Upon returning to office, Donald Trump wasted little time fulfilling his white supremacist campaign pledge of “Mass Deportations Now.” Via a flurry of executive orders and congressional acts his administration reinstated the reviled “family separation” policy; directed virtually unlimited resources to stop a fictitious “invasion” of the country’s borders; and sought to end birthright citizenship. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents blitzed Los Angeles in June 2025 with spectacular raids, followed shortly by similar operations in dozens of cities across the country including New York City; Chicago, IL; New Orleans, LA; and Durham, NC. This “shock and awe” strategy culminated in Operation Metro Surge, a months-long invasion of the Minnesota Twin Cities that deported over 2,000 residents. 


Meanwhile, support for the deportation machine plummeted as collective action against it swelled. Everyday people covered their cars, lawns, and lips with the slogan “Abolish ICE;” as of July 2026, nearly 50% of US adults support such a measure. Both May Days since Trump’s second inauguration centered immigrant defense in their celebrations. Rapid-response networks that keep watch for ICE, document kidnappings, and sometimes disrupt them spread wildly. Know-your-rights training flourished at worksites and community centers. Millions of Red Cards–wallet-sized cards outlining the holder’s constitutional protections around interactions with ICE and other police–were distributed at schools, churches, restaurants, and municipal buildings. Children and their parents caged in concentration camps went on hunger strike as constituents bombarded politicians’ hotlines and town halls demanding humanitarian treatment and release outside their walls.


Popular responses in St. Paul and Minneapolis demonstrate the possibilities of mass resistance. Like the Los Angeles Tenant Union’s community defense centers that countered ICE’s Southern California invasion, organizers reactivated dormant neighborhood networks from the 2020 uprising and began building new ones when word spread that Commander-at-Large Greg Bovino was bringing his paramilitary forces to town. Once Operation Metro Surge launched, everyday Minnesotans refined sophisticated systems to track, delay, and disrupt arrests. ICE agents retaliated by killing rapid-responder Renée Good and shooting Julio C. Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan immigrant targeted for deportation. Instead of cowering from the naked clampdown, neighborhood networks coordinated with unions, churches, and other civil societal organizations to shut down their cities on January 23rd. In its wake, Trump ousted Bovino and immigration enforcement plummeted.


But July 2026 saw record high immigrant detentions since Trump’s return to office with little public opposition. What explains it? ICE’s tactical shifts undoubtedly played a role. Bovino replacement and “Border Czar” Tom Homan traded provocative street operations with quiet detainers at jails and prisons and “targeted operations” at sites protected from activist impediment like airports. Escalating repression has also raised the costs of resistance. ICE’s bevy of brutality has included intimidation, beatings, and shootings, culminating in murdering Good and rapid-responder Alex Pretti. Federal grand juries fish from the shadows for information about our movements, stoking fears of informants that slow our organizing. From the Prairieland defendants to the Minnesota 15 and more, indictments and convictions on flimsy charges could make prosecuting dissidents even easier. Evidentiary discovery in the …

author: Elizabeth Weill-Greenberg
title: Tablets Make Communication Easier Behind Bars – But Deaf People Are Left Behind
content:
This story was co-published with


Truthout

.


Tablet computers have revolutionized communication inside prisons for hearing prisoners. Prison systems from across the country — including in

New York

,

California

, and

Illinois

 — have

distributed tens of thousands

 of tablets to incarcerated people, which they can use to call home, watch movies, message loved ones, or attend virtual classes (although they are often

charged predatory fees

 for accessing these benefits). As of 2022,

25 state prison systems

 had tablet distribution programs, according to the Electronic Privacy Information Center. 


But as the rollout of such tablets continues, many deaf incarcerated people have been left behind. 


Disability justice organization HEARD points out that

it’s

unknown

 how many deaf people are incarcerated in U.S. prisons, but a

2015 report

 by the Bureau of Labor Statistics estimated that 6.2 percent of incarcerated people in

state

 and

federal

 prisons have a hearing disability, which would equal about 71,000 people.


Daniel Valenzuela, who is deaf, is incarcerated at Danville Correctional Center in Illinois. Last year, the Illinois Department of Corrections (IDOC)

distributed tablets

 to all incarcerated people. But IDOC blocks videophone capabilities, preventing Valenzuela from communicating in his primary language, American Sign Language (ASL).  


In September, Valenzuela sued the IDOC director for violating the Americans with Disabilities Act.


“I have six kids, four grandkids, and one of my sons is in the military. I cherish and love my family so much,” said Valenzuela in a

press release

 announcing the lawsuit. “I just want to tell them happy birthday and I am so grieved when I can’t call because I don’t want them to think I forgot.”


There are at least three other deaf individuals at Danville who primarily use ASL to communicate, according to the

complaint

 filed by Disability Rights Advocates, Equip for Equality, and the law firm Much Shelist. 


“Across the Illinois Department of Corrections, people can use tablets to communicate with their loved ones, which has been a game changer in removing restrictions on communication,” Valenzuela’s attorney, Rachel Weisberg, the directing attorney at Disability Rights Advocates, told

Truthout

. “But for Mr. Valenzuela and other deaf people who use American Sign Language, that same access simply isn’t available.” 


IDOC did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication.


Last year, in addition to distributing tablets to incarcerated people, IDOC

announced

 it would provide every incarcerated person with 775 free domestic phone call minutes per month. In a press release,

IDOC said

 that these initiatives, working in tandem, “enhance family connections and increase access to technology that supports rehabilitation.” 


But deaf prisoners are excluded from accessing these critical programs. 


Unlike hearing prisoners who can use their tablets to make calls from their cells, Valenzuela must get a guard’s permission to walk to another building to use the one videophone that’s available to him. In at least one instance, Valenzuela had to go out in the pouring rain to use the videophone, according to the complaint. 


“When prison officials don’t communicate with deaf/disabled people in ways they can understand, they may be written up for being ‘non-compliant.'”


The videophone is often unavailable because the unit itself breaks down, the prison is on lockdown, or a guard denies his request, according to the complaint. Last year, Valenzuela was unable to speak with his family during the holidays because the phone was not working for 54 straight days, from November 2025 to January 2026. However, if the tablets malfunction, there are several backup phones that incarcerated hearing people can use, the complaint says.


“We’re asking for equal access, as that’s what the law requires,” said Weisberg. “Equal access is not static — it must reflect the benefits currently offered to others and account for the needs of people with disabilities as technology and communication systems evolve.”


These issues are not limited to Illinois. Advocates say incarcerated deaf people have to contend with discriminatory communication practices in prisons throughout the country.


“In prisons where we’ve seen scores of deaf/disabled people, there may only be 2 videophones,” Kah Mendoza, the communications coordinator for

HEARD

, told …

title: White Nationalists Off Secwépemc Territory
content:
There is a growing white supremacist genocide denial movement in so-called Canada.

On September 27th members of the Second Sons, a white nationalist militia, marched on unceded Secwépemc territory carrying racist banners near a former residential school where mass graves of Indigenous children were discovered.

This action was timed to occur three days before National Truth and Reconciliation Day a flawed and limited attempt to acknowledge Canada’s genocide of Indigenous peoples.

The Second Sons are tightly connected to the so-called ‘Active Clubs’ movement and have called to remove non-white people from Canada at gunpoint.

The Secwépemc have a long history of resistance to Canadian colonialism, including the Gustaffson Lake standoff in 1995, and more recently, the Tiny House Warrior movement, launched in resistance to the TransMountain Pipeline project.

White supremacy is inherent to settler colonialism.

Settler anarchists have a special responsibility to support Indigenous sovereignty and confront white nationalists wherever they rear their ugly heads.

Get together. Crew up. Confront white supremacy in all its forms.

author: Natalia Viana
title: Foragido, líder do garimpo ilegal Rodrigo Cataratas tem empresas e bens de luxo nos EUA
content:
No Brasil, Rodrigo Cataratas gosta de manter um perfil espalhafatoso nas redes sociais. Condenado na primeira instância por liderar o garimpo ilegal na Terra Indígena Yanomami, ele tem mais de 43 mil seguidores no Instagram, onde defende a garimpagem, pede anistia para o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (preso por tentativa de golpe de Estado) e ataca o governo do PT. 


Mas Rodrigo Martins de Mello – seu nome verdadeiro – é bem mais discreto sobre um aspecto importante da sua vida: seus bens de luxo e suas atividades empresariais nos Estados Unidos, país que frequenta desde os anos 90. Agora sabemos o porquê de tamanha discrição. 


Em dezembro de 2025, o ministro do Supremo Tribunal Federal Alexandre de Moraes decretou a prisão preventiva de Cataratas por ter ajudado na fuga de Alexandre Ramagem, o ex-diretor da Abin do governo Bolsonaro condenado pela trama golpista. Seu pedido de habeas corpus foi negado pela ministra Carmem Lúcia na última terça-feira (19/10), segundo informação do

site Amado Mundo

 confirmada pela

Agência Pública

. “Consta que o mandado de prisão está pendente de cumprimento, pela ausência de localização do paciente até esta data”, escreveu a ministra na decisão. O pedido de prisão preventiva só veio à público nesta semana, já que o processo corre em sigilo.


Pela primeira vez, suas redes estão em silêncio. “Ele sumiu do mapa”, relatou um ex-parceiro de negócios nos EUA localizado pela

Pública

.


Uma investigação conjunta da

Pública

 e do ICIJ (Consórcio Internacional de Jornalistas Investigativos) encontrou rastros do empresário do garimpo ilegal e de sua vida nos Estados Unidos. Ele tem registro de votação como Republicano na Flórida, onde apenas cidadãos norte-americanos podem votar, e manteve empresas ligadas a seu nome e ao de parentes e colegas. Os negócios, todos na Flórida, vão de aluguel de iates à demolição, passando pelo e-commerce.


Uma das empresas ligadas a Cataratas é a X One Charters LLC, fundada em 10 de julho de 2023 e registrada no endereço do apartamento do condomínio Sole Mia, em Miami – onde Cataratas hospedou Ramagem em setembro de 2025, como

revelou a

Pública

. Segundo o documento de fundação da companhia, Cataratas era o dono da empresa. Mas em janeiro de 2026, um mês depois do pedido de prisão preventiva, os registros foram atualizados e ele saiu da sociedade, que passou a ter como diretor Marcos Felix Ribeiro.


Embora no papel a empresa hoje pertença Ribeiro, o WhatsApp de contato do site é um número de Roraima que pertence ao próprio Rodrigo Cataratas.


A empresa foi fundada na época em que Cataratas atuava, segundo o Ministério Público Federal, como um dos líderes de um grupo criminoso responsável por garimpo ilegal e degradação ambiental na

Terra Indígena Yanomami

. Ele foi condenado a 16 anos de prisão e ao pagamento de uma indenização no valor de R$ 31 milhões, mas recorreu e aguarda em liberdade.


A X One Charters oferece aluguel do iate de mesmo nome, segundo

seu site

. O valor pode variar entre R$ 500 mil e R$ 1,2 milhão por algumas horas nas águas de Miami. A embarcação conta com quarto, sala, cozinha e uma área externa de lazer. “Uma embarcação confortável com muitos assentos e acomodações. Cabine espaçosa com AC e banheiro. Sistema de som Premium com Bluetooth para seu entretenimento e tapete aquático para nadar enquanto você aprecia a incrível vista do horizonte da cidade de Miami a partir das águas. Venha conosco para uma experiência incrível”, diz o site, que pode ser lido em inglês, espanhol ou português. Nas fotos, grupos de turistas se deleitam nas águas azuladas da Flórida.


Na mesma alteração nos registros realizada em janeiro de 2026, o endereço da X One Charters mudou. Em vez do Sole Mia, a empresa agora fica sediada em um rancho de 34 acres, o Sunniland Ranch, de propriedade do mesmo Marcos Felix Ribeiro. Procurado pela

Pública

, ele confirmou ter tido transações comerciais com Cataratas em um negócio de mineração na Guiana. Segundo ele, o iate foi dado a ele como pagamento por uma escavadeira sua que ficou no país sulamericano – uma troca estimada em cerca de R$ 500 mil reais (US$ 100 mil).


“Eu peguei esse barco que na realidade é um pesadelo, porque está com problema de vazamento de óleo, um barco desse aqui na água, é 15 mil dólares de multa. Eu tive que tirar esse trambolho da água e no final vai sair mais caro”, diz.


Marcos Felix disse à

Pública

 que conheceu Cataratas quando ele estava com frequência nos EUA, por …

author: Andrés
title: “Justicia es que no vuelva a pasar”: el juicio por el triple lesbicidio de Barracas se acerca a su final
content:
Foto: Sol Erazo


El juicio por el triple lesbicidio de Barracas se acerca al final y convocan a seguir las audiencias. El 6 de mayo de 2024 Justo Fernando Barrientos lanzó un explosivo a la habitación de Barracas donde dormían dos parejas de mujeres lesbianas: Pamela Cobas, Roxana Figueroa, Andrea Amarante y Sofía Castro Riglos. Sofía es la única que sobrevivió. La causa judicial derivada de ese ataque lesboodiante y misógino llegó a Tribunales el pasado 18 de mayo caratulado como “homicidio”. Fue por  impulso de las querellas que ahora se juzga más precisamente como lo que fue: un triple asesinato cometido por el “odio a la orientación sexual de las víctimas, mediando violencia de género”.

Por Sol Tobia, para ANRed. 


Ahora el juicio está por llegar a su fin.

El jueves 15 de octubre declaró el lesbofemicida y restan tres audiencias de alegatos. El lunes 26, protagonizada por las representantes de las víctimas; el miércoles 28, con declaración de la querella colectiva que impulsó la FALGBT, y la tercera con fecha a definir, donde se presentará la defensa del asesino.

 Después, los jueces darán su veredicto y la expectativa es que dicten prisión perpetua. “Sin embargo, más allá de la pena en números, lo que está en juego acá es que se consideren los agravantes por odio a la orientación sexual y por razón de género, además de la alevosía”, explica

Miriam Djeordjian, integrante de la Coordinadora Lesbicidios Nunca Más.


“Se demostró que hubo premeditación para lanzar el artefacto incendiario, que aparentemente fue algún tipo de pintura con un acelerante, y

la saña con la que el agresor, después de arrojar el objeto, bloqueó la puerta para evitar que las compañeras pudieran escapar. Las golpeó para que volvieran a quedar encerradas, y trabó la puerta.

Si no hubiera sido por la intervención de los vecinos, no hubieran ni siquiera logrado salir de la pieza”.


La Coordinadora que integra Djeordjian se formó poco antes del comienzo del juicio y, desde entonces, las mujeres que la integran

concentraron frente al Palacio de Tribunales durante cada audiencia

y realizaron otras actividades de visibilización, tales como llevar la causa al reciente Encuentro Plurinacional que se hizo en Córdoba

. Una de sus principales consignas es que este crimen de odio no se repita más, entendiendo que

 justicia es que no vuelva a pasar

”, detalla la activista.


Foto: Miriam Djordjian


El triple lesbicidio en contexto: misoginia, lesboodio y precarización


Los crímenes como el triple lesbicidio nunca son casos aislados. La misoginia propia de la cultura patriarcal se materializa, entre muchas otras maneras, en los femicidios que los hombres cometen todos los días, y suele tener un agregado específico contra las lesbianas: el odio que despierta en los agresores el hecho de que las mujeres rechacemos el mandato de la heterosexualidad, pilar fundamental del patriarcado.


“

Existió otro ataque en Cañuelas, unos seis o siete meses después

”, recuerda Miriam. Se refiere a lo ocurrido el 29 de enero de 2025, cuando

Orlando Alcides Lutz Fogar, “un nazi que venía amenazando a dos madres lesbianas con una niña”, terminó incendiándoles la casa.

Aquel día “ellas, por sentir miedo, decidieron no pasar la noche en la casa y por eso salvaron su vida”, recuerda la activista y añade que

el juicio por este otro caso está por comenzar en La Plata.


Destaca también

 el asesinato de la Pepa Gaitán en Córdoba, en 2010.

Entonces “no existían en el Código Penal las agravantes que hoy sí existen. El padrastro de su novia, 

Daniel Torres, que la fusila con varios disparos a corta distancia, fue condenado a 14 años de prisión, de los cuales terminó cumpliendo solo ocho, y hoy está libre”. A continuación, menciona

 “el ataque que sufrió Higui”, quien estuvo presa por defenderse de “una violación correctiva”,

 y salió en libertad gracias a la lucha de las organizaciones que la acompañaron.


Sofía Castro Riglos, única sobreviviente de la masacre lesboodiante, presenciando la audiencia virtual de la defensa del asesino frente a Palacio de Tribunales el pasado 15 de octubre. Foto: Sol Erazo


El anhelo de quienes integran la Coordinadora es que el triple lesbicidio de Barracas se reconozca como parte de un continuo de violencia lesboodiante, sirviendo además para el futuro: “

author: CMI Argentina
title: Neuquén: jurado popular encontró culpable a Roberto Sánchez por el transfemicidio de Azul Semeñenko
content:
Un jurado popular declaró culpable a Roberto Daniel Sánchez por el homicidio de Azul Semeñenko, triplemente agravado por ensañamiento, odio a su identidad de género y mediado por violencia de género. Se trató de un juicio histórico en la provincia de Neuquén, que se desarrolló a lo largo de 12 audiencias y contó con más de 30 testimonios.


Escuchar el reporte de La Revuelta y Periodistas Feministas


Durante las jornadas, compañeras de trabajo de Azul, organizaciones feministas, integrantes de la comunidad LGBTIQ+ y organizaciones sociales acompañaron el proceso. En la última audiencia, estuvieron presentes con un altar en homenaje a Azul, carteles y música.


Tras conocerse el veredicto, su hermano,

Marco Millapán

, destacó el acompañamiento colectivo y la importancia de la decisión judicial.

“La verdad que haber conseguido este veredicto del jurado popular es fruto colectivo de cada uno de los que hoy están presentes y de los que nos han venido acompañando a lo largo de todo este año”

, expresó.


“Logramos lo que todos queríamos, justicia por y para Azul. Esto fue un transfemicidio, esto fue un crimen de odio”

, afirmó.


Por su parte, el fiscal jefe

Agustín García

 señaló que el juicio implicó un importante desafío por la cantidad y complejidad de las pruebas presentadas.

“Fue un juicio en donde había mucha información, muchos testigos, muchos peritos. Había que trabajarlo de tal modo que toda esa prueba fuera bien comprendida por el jurado, en el contexto en que se dan las cosas, acá no se puede aislar hechos individuales sin contextualizarlo”

, explicó.


García también remarcó la relevancia del reconocimiento de las agravantes:

“El primer caso en Neuquén, en donde desde la reforma del año 2012 se juzga a una persona con estas agravantes, era un desafío también para nosotros”

.


El homicidio ocurrió durante la madrugada del 25 de septiembre de 2025 dentro de la vivienda de Sánchez, situada en la ciudad de Neuquén. De acuerdo con la acusación, dentro de la casa Sánchez atacó a Azul con golpes realizados con elementos contundentes y con un arma blanca. La autopsia confirmó que la víctima recibió 25 heridas de arma blanca.


Desde la querella valoraron el veredicto como un alivio para la familia, después de atravesar un largo proceso en busca de justicia.

“Hoy es una brisa también que alivia un poco el fuego en el que se viven las injusticias, como venía viviendo la familia hasta este día”

, expresaron.


Además, remarcaron que la decisión del jurado debe generar una reflexión social:

“Declararon que fue un transfemicidio, pero esto tiene que construir también un aprendizaje a nuestra comunidad. Azul no nos la devuelven, pero Azul tiene que ser la última”

.


Tras la declaración de culpabilidad de Sánchez, se espera que en los próximos días se realice la audiencia de determinación de la pena.


Fuente:

https://agencia.farco.org.ar/2026/10/20/97144/

Neuquén: jurado popular encontró culpable a Roberto Sánchez por el transfemicidio de Azul Semeñenko

 se publicó primero en

Indymedia Argentina Centro de Medios Independientes (( i ))

.

author: Darío Aranda
title: Elecciones en Brasil: deforestación, frontera agrícola y ultraderecha
content:
Por Raúl Zibechi


“La frontera agrícola avanza expropiando, y la expropiación necesita de apoyo político”, escribe el abogado en derechos humanos Diogo Cabral en un trabajo que cruza datos para intentar comprender dónde y cómo se produce el avance de la ultraderecha bolsonarista, concentrado en la selva amazónica. Las conclusiones de su trabajo son tremendas y pueden ser resumidas en el editorial de Eliane Brum, directora del sitio periodístico Sumaúma: si Flávio Bolsonaro vence en la segunda vuelta, describe Brum, “existe una gran posibilidad de que la selva deje de existir como tal, lo que implica que dejará de actuar como reguladora del clima y sumidero de carbono, uno de los gases responsables del calentamiento global”.


El bolsonarismo gobernará siete de los nueve estados de la Amazonia, en tanto más de la mitad de los parlamentarios electos ya han votado en contra de la selva y de los pueblos originarios, según

la investigación de Sumaúma

.


Esta realidad impone colocar la lupa sobre lo que sucede en la Amazonia Legal brasileña, (Mato Grosso, Pará, Rondônia, Tocantins, Maranhão, Acre, Amapá, Amazonas y Roraima), que ocupa el 60 por ciento del total de la selva amazónica. En las últimas cuatro décadas la territorialidad del conflicto por la tierra se ha movido desde el sureste, donde nació el

Movimiento de Trabajadores Rurales Sin Tierra (MST)

, migró primero hacia el norte y nordeste, y ahora hacia la Amazonia, siguiendo los pasos de la expansión del agronegocio.


La expansión ha sido geométrica:

en 1990 había


once


millones de hectáreas cultivadas de soja, llegando a casi 50 millones en la actualidad

; la producción del grano creció 738 por ciento en los últimos 40 años, en tanto el área sembrada se expandió en un

322


por ciento


en el mismo período

. Hacia finales de la década de 1970, más del 80 por ciento de la soja provenía de los estados del sur; en la década siguiente comenzó a extenderse por la región central (Mato Grosso, Goiás y el distrito de Brasilia). Esta región que hace 40 años representaba el dos por ciento de la producción nacional de soja, ahora alcanza el 40 por ciento.


Este cambio notable puede observarse en el mapa

(ver mapa)

, donde se combinan cuatro variables analíticas: la deforestación, los conflictos agrarios de 2025 registrados por la

Comisión Pastoral de la Tierra (CPT)

, el monitoreo de la pulverización con agrotóxicos de la Red de Agroecología de Maranhão y los resultados electorales de la primera vuelta.


En color azul los lugares donde ganó Bolsonario. En rojo donde triunfó Lula


A medida que la frontera agrícola se expande, el mapa se va coloreando de azul.

José de Souza Martino, citado por Cabral

, entiende la frontera agrícola no sólo como la línea de avance de la producción agropecuaria sobre la vegetación nativa, sino como “espacio social de conflictos”. Se trata de una expansión autoritaria, “acumulación por despojo” como la definiera David Harvey, que busca convertir la tierra en mercancía para lo que debe no sólo apropiársela sino expulsar a las comunidades indígenas, quilombolas (negras) y pueblos tradicionales.


Datos crudos e impunidad


Los datos indican que entre 2019 y 2025 Brasil perdió once millones de hectáreas de vegetación nativa, siendo la actividad agropecuaria la responsable del 97 por ciento de esa deforestación. En paralelo, se registra un promedio de 1.500 conflictos en el campo; con 26 asesinatos en 2025, el doble que en el año anterior, y los hacendados fueron responsables de 14 de las 16 muertes en la Amazonia Legal. En los 34 años en los cuales la CPT viene sistematizando datos de conflictos rurales, hubo casi

2.000


asesinatos, pero sólo 120 habían sido juzgados hasta 2018

, según la CPT.


Flávio Bolsonaro tuvo sus mayores votaciones justamente en los estados donde la deforestación fue más intensa: 71 por ciento en Roraima, 67 por ciento en Rondonia, 65 por ciento en Mato Grosso y en Acre. “Ganó en ocho de los diez municipios de la Amazonia Legal que más deforestaron desde 2016”, asegura Cabral, cruzando datos electorales y del Instituto Nacional de Investigaciones Espaciales, que monitorea las áreas deforestadas.


Foto: Pedro Saldanha Werneck - Mídia NINJA


La ciudad de Novo Progresso, en Pará, que en 2019 fue el epicentro del “Día del Fuego” (10 de agosto, cuando los productores rurales iniciaron la quema masiva de áreas de la selva, para “limpiar” y permitir el avance del agronegocio), Bolsonaro obtuvo el 85 …

author: Administrador
title: Zapatistische Vorbereitungen für das umarmende Treffen mit den Familien Sucherinnen. Teil II. »Plan D«.
content:
»Die Delegation der Reise für das Leben – Kapitel Mexiko beim Ausüben der bekannten Spielvariante »Gemeinschaftlicher Fußball« oder »Massiver Fußball«. Kein Ball erlitt dabei einen Schaden … die Spieler*innen … nun, Ihr seht es im Video.«

Musik: Cuatro Pesos de Propina: »La Verdadera – Die Wahre« und »El Maleficio – Der Fluch«. Aufnahmen, Bearbeitung, Produktion: Terci@s Compas Zapatistas.

Zapatistische Vorbereitungen für das umarmende Treffen mit den Familien Sucherinnen.

Schwestern, Brüder, Schwestern-Brüder* der Familien Sucherinnen.

Compañeras, Compañeros und Compañeroas.

Comunidad originaria Otomí der Casa de los Pueblos Samir Flores Soberanes.

Wir informieren Euch darüber, dass der sogenannte Plan C gescheitert ist. Wir kommen jetzt nicht, wie wir gesagt haben, mit 1.509, nein, wir kommen nun mit 1.530. Hoffen wir, ein Plan E wird nicht notwendig sein, aber mensch weiß ja nie – nachher kommen welche mit dem Trick an: »Wir sind ja nur zum Abschiednehmen hier« – und steigen dann in die Busse: »Tja, nun seht mal zu«.

Wir haben uns als gesamte Delegation versammelt, um uns gut vorzubereiten und Euch ein gutes Wort der Ermutigung und Unterstützung zu bringen.

Viele* von uns können nicht gut castilla [spanisch]. Unsere Muttersprachen sind Maya-Sprachen. Somit müssen wir auch die vorbereiten, die übersetzen werden – und korrigieren, so weit wir können – damit unser Wort nicht falsch und verdreht herauskommt.

Wir sind froh, weil wir Euch zuhören, mit Euch sprechen, Euch umarmen werden können. Somit praktizieren wir. Lediglich die Umarmungen praktizieren wir nicht [vorher], denn wie Ihr wisst, nachher gibt es auf einmal eine*n Clevere*n, der*die befiehlt, das heißt, profitieren will.

Manchmal spielen wir zusammengeballt Fußball, falls dort [in Mexiko-Stadt] ein Spiel organisiert werden sollte.

Innerhalb der Delegation sind wir:

709 Männer, 622 Frauen und 2 Otroas-AnderE*.

24 des Comando Popcorn: 10 Jungen und 14 Mädchen.

110 der Comunidad Jugendliche Gemeinsam: 66 Männer und 43 Frauen. [Gesamtzahl?]

27 der Koordinierungsequipe: 7 Frauen und 20 Männer.

39 der Miliz [zapatistische zivile Selbstverteidigungsstruktur]: 16 Milicianos und 23 Milicianas.

Bis heute, 18. Oktober 2026, sind es insgesamt, ungefähr, 1.530 Delegierte* sowie verflixte Rasselbande aus Mädchen und Jungen. Somit seht zu.

Für den Moment ist das alles, Compañeras, Compañeroas und Compañeros, Schwestern-Brüder*, Brüder und Schwestern.

Falls es eine Änderung gibt (wir beten, es gibt keine), sagen wir Euch Bescheid. Wir werden Euch weitere Videos schicken, wie wir uns am Vorbereiten sind.

Wir senden Euch unsere gemeinschaftliche Umarmung, darauf hoffend, sie Euch bald persönlich zu geben.

Aus den Bergen des Südosten Mexikos.

Subcomandante Insurgente Moisés. Hauptkoordinator der Reise für das Leben – Kapitel Mexiko.
