author: Anikibawal
title: Comunicado de los PPM del Módulo comuneros de la Cárcel de Temuco tras el llamado a Marcha por la Resistencia, el 12 de octubre pasado.
content:
Comunicado de los presos políticos Mapuche del Módulo Comuneros de la Cárcel de Temuco tras el llamado a movilización Marcha por la resistencia, del pasado lunes 12 de octubre.


«Nosotros los prisioneros políticos mapuche recluidos en la cárcel de temuko saludamos a nuestras autoridades tradicionales y a todos quienes fueron participe de la gran movilización llevada adelante, el lunes 12 de octubre en la ciudad de temuko.


Mediante este escrito, venimos a agradecer la gran convocatoria realizada este 12 de octubre en apoyo concreto a los PPM de la cárcel de Temuco y a sus demandas, por parte del movimiento social en toda su amplitud.


Agradecemos a todos aquellos y aquellas que pusieron sus ganas y newen para que todo resultara de la mejor manera: a nuestros familiares, pu afkadi, autoridades tradicionales, comunidades en resistencia de diversos puntos del wallmapu, wenuy y simpatizantes de nuestra causa.


Hoy, a días de la gran movilización, creemos que esta logró los objetivos esperados con creces. Por tanto, agradecemos a nuestro pueblo por demostrar su fuerza cuando se lo propone.


La unidad en el weichan la entendemos como aquella en la que todo nuestro pueblo tiene su espacio, en sus distintas formas, con sus aciertos y errores. Aquí tienen cabida todos quienes busquen ser partícipes de la unidad que, como pueblo mapuche, merecemos darnos. Desde el pichiche hasta los kuifiche, todo nuestro pueblo tiene su espacio cuando se trata de levantar un movimiento social mapuche sólido, capaz de reunir la fuerza necesaria para luchar por lo que nos pertenece.


Eso sí, esta unidad debe construirse siempre desde la transparencia y la honestidad, sin dar cabida a los personalismos ni a las supuestas cualidades morales particulares.


Reconocemos también a cada uno de los peñi, ka pu lamngen y wenny de la causa mapuche que destinaron un día que podrían haber utilizado para descansar o compartir con sus familias en casa, y que, en cambio, se dieron el ánimo de asistir para expresar su solidaridad consciente con los familiares y los PPM.


Extendemos, finalmente, nuestros agradecimientos a todo el movimiento social mapuche que, cuando se lo propone, demuestra que es posible confluir en ideas y aspiraciones que aglutinan y suman. Esto cobra especial relevancia en los tiempos que corren, en los que la atomización y el individualismo prevalecen por sobre la justa intención de juntarse y organizarse, con el propósito de ser partícipes concretos del movimiento social mapuche autónomo.


Fei taiñ feipiaiñ may. Chaltu may kom eimun!¡¡KIÑEWKULEAIÑ WEICHAN MEW!!


Fin a las altas condenas


Fin a la dispersión de los PPM.


Fin al estado de excepción en Wall Mapu.


No a la aplicación de la ley Antiterrorista.


A más de 500 años de resistencia no pudieron ni podrán borrar la memoria del mapuzungun. «


*Enviado a la radio.


Esta información se publicó en

Radio Kurruf

.

author: La Zarzamora
title: DESPEDIR A JUAN…
content:
Esta mañana nuestro compañero Juan Aliste Vega ha partido de su cuerpo, cuerpo que el poder mantuvo en encierro los últimos 16 años, cuerpo que practicó el conflicto y lo materializó en acciones armadas, que acompañó su vida en el álgido recorrido de ser él. Fue en el hospital penitenciario de Santiago, donde en compañia y calma, se fugó definitivamente.

Aún no podemos confirmar donde ni como será su despedida, ló que sí sabemos es que serán muchas, en muchos territorios, en las calles, en los puentes, en las jaulas, en avenidas y carreteras.

Juan Aliste es y será reivindicado, pese a los esfuerzos incansables de la prensa del enemigo y de sus múltiples intentos de desprestigiarlo, nosotrxs sus compañerxs sabemos que en este momento estamos despidiendo a un guerrero de gran envergadura. Pese a sus miserables conjunciones de palabras, el mundo sabe quien es Juan y en todos los territorios se levantará fuego en su memoria.

Que desesperanza deben sentir los poderosos, al saber que amamos pese a estar en guerra, que nuestra historia es escrita por nosotrxs, pese a sus asquerosos relatos oficiales, tan indignos como ellos mismos.

Hoy es un día de nuestra propia historia, hoy parte el guerrero combatiente que se alzó en armas contra la dictadura y la pestilente democracia de burgueses y traidores, el que no se dejó abatir, el que atacó y acertó, el que siguió compartiendo conocimientos y enseñanzas pese al encierro, el que enviaba notas y saludos, el que hacía llegar sus palabras a actividades y espacios.

Cada vez es más difícil despedir, esto no es una noticia, ni tampoco un comunicado, es nuestro adiós a un hermano…

A nosotrxs ahora nos quedará volver a mirarnos, tensionar el encierro de nuestrxs compañerxs, cuestionarnos y autocriticarnos, dejar de hacernos tolerantes al encarcelamiento, dejar de normalizar la sociedad carcelaria y hacer. Arduo camino nos dejas.

Juan que tu fuga sea eterna querido compañero.

Ternura y ataque frontal por ti y por todxs nuestrxs muertxs.

author: Marcelo Oliveira
title: Ministério Público encurrala Meta para barrar bloqueios e restrições nas eleições
content:
Em dois movimentos distintos, um judicial e outro extrajudicial,

o Ministério Público Federal (MPF) quer barrar bloqueios, suspensões de contas e restrições de alcance promovidos pela Meta no Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp e Threads.


Na Justiça Federal do Rio Grande do Sul, o MPF ajuizou nesta quarta-feira, 21 de outubro, uma ação civil pública, com pedido de urgência. Em outra frente, a Procuradoria Federal dos Direitos do Cidadão (PFDC) enviou recomendação à Meta, cobrando providências imediatas.


A ação lida especificamente com as denúncias que fazem parte da representação feita pelas organizações Ctrl+Z, Artigo 19, Conectas e Sleeping Giants Brasil, que mostram que a Meta bloqueou conteúdos políticos pró-Lula e contra Flávio. A

Agência Pública


mostrou

 que além dos bloqueios,

a plataforma derrubou perfis com acusação de terrorismo e nudez, mesmo não havendo conteúdos nesse sentido.

 A Procuradoria pede o restabelecimento imediato de contas, páginas e conteúdos afetados pelas restrições apontadas na representação.


A ação pede ainda que a Justiça Federal proíba o uso exclusivo de algoritmos para decisões de bloqueio de conteúdo e que as futuras reavaliações e análises de recursos sejam conduzidas obrigatoriamente por equipes humanas especializadas

, com a fixação de multa diária de R$ 500 mil por conta afetada, em caso de descumprimento.


O MPF apurou que as restrições arbitrárias impostas pela companhia foram operadas por meio de algoritmos automatizados, sem notificação clara sobre as supostas violações ou oportunidade de contestação por canal efetivo com revisão humana. Essa prática provocou o enfraquecimento do engajamento de conteúdos cívicos e o cerceamento do debate democrático.


Ao público, no dia 16, a Meta

reconheceu

 que “a conta de anúncios da campanha de Lula foi desativada por engano por pouco mais de 1 hora”, mas afirmou que não se tratou de “razões políticas”.


Após pedir para ‘Flávio abrir o sigilo’, dona de comunidade é bloqueada pela Meta


Uma das vítimas das restrições foi a arquiteta Carolina Martins, 43, de Brasília. Ela criou um grupo e uma comunidade visando angariar apoio para a candidatura de Lula no segundo turno. O grupo chegou a ser derrubado, acusado de “terrorismo” sem fundamentação pela empresa. Ela teve a conta de WhatsApp derrubada e ainda está sofrendo outras restrições da Meta.


Ao divulgar esta semana a proposta do presidente Lula para que ambos os candidatos abram seu sigilo bancário, feita após o

debate

 da rede Bandeirantes,

Martins postou uma imagem que dizia “Flavio Abra o Sigilo”. Na segunda-feira, dia 19, ela foi suspensa pela Meta de postar links em suas publicações no Instagram até 16 de novembro sob a acusação de “práticas comerciais proibidas”.


Recomendação quer resposta da Meta em 48 horas


Já a recomendação, que é uma medida extrajudicial para uma empresa ou ente público realizar medidas para corrigir uma ilegalidade, foi expedida pela Procuradoria Federal dos Direitos do Cidadão, em Brasília, e direcionada diretamente à Meta para que a companhia adote medidas urgentes de transparência e proteção à liberdade de expressão nas redes Facebook, Instagram, Threads e WhatsApp durante o período eleitoral.


À empresa foi dado prazo de 48 horas para responder se acatará as recomendações do MPF e para detalhar as providências que serão adotadas durante o segundo turno das eleições, além de 30 dias para apresentar um relatório conclusivo.


A medida da PFDC vem depois da instauração de investigação no último dia 13 na qual o MPF pediu à Meta uma série de informações. A companhia enviou uma resposta ao MPF no dia 19 de outubro, complementada ontem, 20. 


Nas respostas, segundo a PFDC, a Meta teria alegado, em síntese, que a sua moderação se basearia nos Padrões da Comunidade e na legislação local, que não levaria em conta a orientação política ou ideológica dos usuários.


As respostas foram consideradas genéricas pelo MPF e não abordaram as moderações indevidas e não esclareceram caso a caso no que se baseou cada restrição, conforme demandado no ofício da semana passada.


A manifestação da Meta não mencionou as suspensões fundadas em enquadramentos graves (como terrorismo e abuso sexual), nem das remoções que teriam ocorrido após denúncias em massa. A recomendação à Meta é assinada pelo Procurador Federal dos Direitos do Cidadão, Paulo Thadeu Gomes da Silva, e mais cinco procuradores do MPF que atuam na área de direitos humanos.

author: anred
title: ATE marcha a la Quinta de Olivos contra los retiros voluntarios: «se endeudan en dólares para despedir en pesos»
content:
Imagen: Prensa ATE.


La Asociación Trabajadores del Estado (ATE) se movilizará este miércoles 21 de octubre a las 17 a la Quinta Presidencial de Olivos contra el régimen de retiros voluntarios para empleados de la Administración Pública Nacional que quiere imponer el gobierno de Javier Milei. El sindicato denuncia que el gobierno nacional aprobó un préstamo de hasta 300 millones de dólares con el Banco Interamericano de Desarrollo (BID) para financiar el programa que, informó el sindicato, alcanzaría a 21.187 trabajadores y establece que quienes adhieran no podrán volver al Sector Público Nacional durante ocho años. «Se endeudan en dólares para despedir en pesos. Esto es un disparate, una maniobra completamente ilegal. Los vamos a ir a buscar a Olivos porque a la Casa Rosada no van nunca a laburar. Este Gabinete está lleno de vagos», afirmó el secretario general de ATE Nacional, Rodolfo Aguiar. Bajo la consigna «No se aguanta más», el gremio estatal también reclama contra los despidos, la pérdida del poder adquisitivo, las paritarias por debajo de la inflación y el cierre y vaciamiento de organismos públicos.

Por ANRed.


La

Asociación Trabajadores del Estado (ATE)

 se movilizará este

miércoles 21 de octubre, a las 17, a la Quinta Presidencial de Olivos

 contra el

régimen de retiros voluntarios para empleados de la Administración Pública Nacional

. Bajo la consigna “No se aguanta más”, el sindicato cuestiona que el Gobierno de

Javier Milei haya habilitado un préstamo de hasta 300 millones de dólares con el Banco Interamericano de Desarrollo (BID) en el marco de su «programa de transformación del Estado»

, que ATE vincula con el financiamiento de las desvinculaciones laborales.


“

Los vamos a ir a buscar a Olivos porque a la Casa Rosada no van nunca a laburar. Este Gabinete está lleno de vagos

.

Ningún país del mundo se endeuda para achicarse, sino para tener un mejor futuro

. Estos se endeudan para destruir”, afirmó el secretario general de ATE Nacional,

Rodolfo Aguiar

, al anunciar la movilización. El dirigente también manifestó: “

Se endeudan en dólares para despedir en pesos

. Esto es un disparate, una maniobra completamente ilegal”.


Imagen: prensa ATE


El préstamo fue aprobado mediante el

Decreto 1177/2026

, publicado el 14 de octubre, que habilitó la firma de un contrato con el BID por hasta 300 millones de dólares para el programa “Transformación del Estado Nacional I”, en el marco de una línea de crédito condicional de hasta 800 millones. El organismo internacional describe sus objetivos como la mejora de la gestión del empleo público y el fortalecimiento de la capacidad tecnológica de la Administración Pública Nacional. Si bien ATE denuncia que el endeudamiento financiará los retiros, el decreto encuadra formalmente el crédito en un programa más amplio de modernización estatal.


Decreto 1177/2026


El régimen de retiros voluntarios quedó oficializado mediante el

Decreto 1203/2026,

 publicado el 19 de octubre.

Según informó ATE, el universo potencialmente alcanzado es de 21.187 trabajadores y quienes adhieran no podrán reincorporarse al Sector Público Nacional durante ocho años y los cargos que dejen vacantes serán suprimidos

. El programa comprende personal de planta permanente de la Administración Pública Nacional centralizada y trabajadores contratados por tiempo indeterminado bajo la Ley de Contrato de Trabajo.


En este marco, desde el sindicato estatal, remarcan: “

desde ATE desalentamos cualquier tipo de adhesión a este régimen extorsivo. Estos retiros son una estafa

”, sostuvo Aguiar. El sindicato cuestiona especialmente las condiciones de adhesión y afirma que quienes tienen mandato sindical vigente o son candidatos a delegados deben renunciar a esa función para acceder al régimen. Para la organización,

esas condiciones restringen derechos laborales y sindicales y convierten una salida formalmente voluntaria en un mecanismo de presión sobre quienes trabajan en el Estado

.


El secretario general de ATE también cuestionó la legalidad del financiamiento: “

esta medida es completamente ilegal. Está prohibido tomar deuda en dólares para gasto corriente. Además, vulnera la Ley de Presupuesto, ya que esta deuda no fue aprobada por el Congreso

”, afirmó. “Están aumentando la deuda externa para dejar sin empleo a los estatales y sin prestaciones y derechos. Con esto, los únicos que ganan son los bancos extranjeros y perdemos todos los argentinos”, agregó Aguiar.

author: Kodao Productions
title: SC ruling declaring Marcos budget unconstitutional vindicates Makabayan
content:
The three progressive legislators who voted against the General Appropriation Act (GAA) of both 2004 and 2005 were vindicated by the Supreme Court decision declaring portions of the budgets unconstitutional, the Makabayan Coalition said.


ACT Teachers Party-list’s France Castro, Gabriela Women’s Party’s Arlene Brosas, and Kabataan Party-list’s Raoul Manuel were the only members of the House of Representatives who voted against both national budgets.


“Makabayan lawmakers have long assailed the budget and the pork barrel corruption that has arisen from it. They have long assailed the [bicameral committee] practices of bloating Unprogrammed Appropriations and budgetary infrastructure insertions,” the coalition said.


In the 2024 GAA ratification, the three former representatives registered their “No” votes citing concerns over huge allocations for unprogrammed funds, confidential and intelligence funds (CIFs), and insufficient funding for social services and public utility sectors.


In the 2025 GAA ratification, they again opposed the report, criticizing the sudden increase in unprogrammed appropriations, lack of transparency in bicameral insertions, and reduced budgets for critical sectors like education and health.


In a decision announced this week, the Supreme Court declared portions of the

budgets unconstitutional, faulting Congress for bloating the budget by P449.5-billion in unprogrammed funds in the 2024 GAA and by P17.99-billion in the DPWH Special Road Fund in the 2025 GAA.


The High Court voided the 2024 GAA

as

 it “unlawfully inflated” the total budget beyond President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s recommended ceiling. The Court also struck down the congressional additions to the 2025 budget.


Invalid 2026 budget provisions


The SC likewise invalidated specific special provisions of the 2026 GAA such as the P12.75-billion increase in “special accounts,” the SAGIP

(

Strengthening Assistance for Government Infrastructure and Social Programs) as an “unconstitutional lump-sum appropriation with post-enactment executive discretion.”


The Court affirmed the prohibition on Congress from increasing the total budget recommended by the President that applies to the combined sum of programmed and unprogrammed appropriations.


The decision clarified that the beneficiaries do not need to return funds under the doctrine of operative fact that assumes the projects were implemented in good faith.


The authors, proposers, or implementers of the unconstitutional items can still face civil, criminal, or administrative charges if they acted in bad faith, however.


Proud of ‘lonely stand’


Manuel said he is proud to be one of only three who took the lonely stand against the unconstitutional budgets.


“As ex-Kabataan Partylist rep, I am honored to have witnessed the efforts of fellow former legislators Arlene Brosas and France Castro in scrutinizing the unprogrammed funds,” he said in a social media post.


Manuel said their decision was supported by the research work of Makabayan Coalition’s congressional staff who flagged so-called unprogrammed funds when they were still being proposed in Congress.


“Even after the budget bills were signed into law by the corrupt president Marcos Jr., progressive groups kept a close watch on the unprogrammed appropriations. This led to the discovery that Marcos Jr. authorized the use of these funds for flood control projects—bypassing Congress and the standard budgetary process,” Manuel pointed out.


“Although we are outnumbered within the House of Representatives—a hotbed for traditional politicians and political dynasties—our advocacies are bearing fruit, thanks to the strength of the Filipino people’s collective struggle outside the halls of Congress,” he added. #

(Raymund B. Villanueva)

author: groundxero
title: Bonus Is Not Charity: Tea Workers in Dooars Demand Unpaid Dues, Justice and Accountability
content:
Six Merico-Sammelan managers are in custody, but the group’s directors and employers remain unarrested. As workers continue to wait for bonus and other outstanding dues, PBCMS demands arrest of owners, recovery of payments, Rs 5,000 relief for workers denied bonus, and protection of abandoned garden assets.


 


20 October 2026 | Groundxero Desk


 


Even after workers took to the streets, blocked highways and forced the authorities to act, thousands of tea garden workers in the Dooars in North Bengal are still waiting for the bonus they were promised before Durga Puja. In a particularly brazen display of political appropriation, the distribution of bonus money in some gardens has been turned into a BJP publicity event, presenting workers’ bonus payment as a favour bestowed by political leaders.


 


Meanwhile, six Merico-Sammelan managers have been arrested and two other managers are reportedly absconding, following cases filed by the Paschim Banga Cha Majdur Samiti (PBCMS), but the directors and employers evade accountability and remain untouched. The arrest of managers has failed to resolve the crisis confronting thousands of workers across tea estates. Five of the arrested managers were due to appear before the Alipurduar court on Tuesday, 20 October, after spending four days in police custody. The question now is whether the police and administration will pursue the cases against the garden owners allegedly responsible for the non-payment of workers’ dues, or whether the action will stop with the managers.


 


The latest developments follow weeks of protests over the failure to pay the promised 20% annual bonus by the government’s 5 October deadline. As documented in Groundxero’s earlier

report

,

“No Bonus, Unpaid Wages, Missing PF Dues: Thousands of Tea Workers Take to the Streets in North Bengal”

 (16 October), the dispute is part of a wider crisis involving unpaid wages, outstanding leave allowances, provident fund contributions allegedly not deposited since June 2023, and gratuity dues owed to retired workers.


Tea workers block highway over withhold bonus


The management’s repeated assurances have not translated into payment. Workers have had to organise demonstrations, march to police stations and block highways to demand money earned through their labour. The arrests mark a development in the struggle, but they do not settle the outstanding dues or establish accountability across the ownership and management of the gardens.


 


PBCMS has demanded that the authorities pursue all cases filed by the union and the Labour Department, recover workers’ outstanding payments and ensure accountability through due process. The union has also called for effective action to secure the arrest of the remaining accused.


 


Bonus is a workers’ right, not BJP’s charity


 


The struggle has also exposed how a workers’ entitlement can be appropriated for political publicity.


 


On 17 October, a 10% bonus (half of the promised of 20%) was distributed in Dumchipara, Hantapara, Gairganda, Tulsipara and Birpara gardens. Workers at Bagrakote, Kilcott and Nageisuree were still waiting for bonus payment.


 


At Samsing tea garden, the distribution of bonus became a ruling party spectacle, with three BJP ministers, two MLAs and an MP present. The MP was seen counting and handing out money amid prominently displayed BJP flags.


BJP leaders distributing bonus to workers


The political message was unmistakable: a payment due to workers was being projected as a favour delivered by the ruling party. But bonus is not charity, nor is it a favour from ministers or MPs or MLAs. It is an entitlement arising from workers’ labour, and its payment should not depend on political patronage or turned into publicity event of a political party.


 


The irony is especially sharp because the BJP government, like the previous Trinamool Congress government, had announced a 20% bonus and set a deadline of October 4-5 for payment. Yet the failure to enforce that deadline has left workers to take to streets to protests to secure their own earnings. The government has failed to effectively enforce its own assurance and take action against employers who deliberately refused to pay the workers their dues.


 


Fresh promises, more unanswered questions


 


Puna Bhengra, BJP MLA from Metelli, has announced that a new owner would pay a 20% bonus in Nageisuree, Kilcott, Bamandanga-Tundu and Samsing. This was followed by assurances of …

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Displaced Marawi survivors still long for justice
content:
Marawi displaced survivor Baiminang Madale speaking in the opening of Alongan sa Marawi exhibit. Photo by Dominic Gutoman/Bulatlat.

More than nine years have passed since the Philippine government declared the “liberation” of Marawi City after the siege that displaced more than 300,000 families. Some of them are now living in different parts of the country, uncertain if they could return.

“We were already familiar with the term bakwit (evacuee/displacement). But the Marawi Siege was different. Before, our bakwit would only last for three days. This time, it feels as though we have been permanently driven out of Marawi,” Baiminang Madale, a displaced Maranao survivor living in Manila, said in the vernacular during the opening of Alongan sa Marawi (One Day in Marawi) exhibit.

The exhibit runs until November 15, 2026, at the Rift Gallery Edsa. It is organized by researchers, journalists, survivors, and advocates to commemorate the ninth year of the city’s so-called liberation. It seeks to provide a visual experience of Marawi from the survivors’ perspective.

“The Maranao, like other tribes and communities, have our own culture, dreams, and lives. Because of the Marawi Siege, we feel as though we have not simply been stripped naked, but forcibly stripped out of our homes that shape our identity,” Madale said. “Marawi is the very heart of the Maranao people. Imagine suddenly losing everything—it is far worse than a nightmare. We never thought something like this could happen to us.”

The Philippine government declared October 17 as Marawi Liberation Day starting in 2017 to mark what it called as a “military victory” against the Islamic State-linked Maute group after a five-month battle.

Madale, who is also part of the board of Ako Bakwit, a group working for the welfare and rights of internally displaced peoples (IDPs), said that there are many more families like hers forced to live in Manila since the siege.

Earlier this year, Bulatlat reported that the displaced families have yet to return to their homes in Marawi. Around 17,000 families or 80,000 individuals are still living in 15 temporary shelters in Marawi and Lanao del Sur, according to Marawi Advocacy Accompaniment.

Read: After 9 years, Marawi displaced families have yet to return to their homes

Under the Marawi Siege Victims Compensation Act of 2022, any owner of a residential, cultural, or commercial structure, and other properties in Marawi’s 24 MAA and eight barangays considered as other affected areas (OAA) is entitled to monetary compensation subject to verification.

Compensation claims, under the law, shall be filed within one year from the date of commencement of the filing (July 4, 2023) to the date of its termination (July 3, 2024).

Read: Group opposes Marawi Siege compensation planned changes

Data from the Marawi Compensation Board (MCB), the government body that awards monetary compensation to eligible claimants, showed that 3,699 claims were resolved from 2023 to June 30, 2026, amounting to P6.154 billion. This is 25.51 percent of the estimated 14,497 total claims to be resolved by the body by 2028.

Mindanao State University Prof. Sorhalia Latip-Yusoph said that the recovery and return process for the survivors are hurdled by a tedious bureaucratic process.

“The government’s requirements for returning are extremely difficult to meet. Sometimes, we do not understand why the process has to be so difficult. Perhaps they want to be strict,” Latip-Yusoph said. “Our fellow Maranaos (in bakwit) are truly the ones who, if we may put it this way, are the reason our hearts continue to ache. Many of them are still living elsewhere. I hope we will not reach the tenth year without being able to return home.”

Task Force Bangon Marawi was a government inter-agency task force group established by former President Rodrigo Duterte in June 2017 to facilitate rehabilitation, recovery, and reconstruction.

However, Madale said that the four stages of the task force’s process did not align with the needs of the IDPs and survivors of the Marawi siege. The process includes registration, mapping, submission of documents, and biometrics. However, most IDPs lack valid identification and their house/land ownership documents– most of the time– are not recognized by the government implementers.

“The process is inhumane. Even application to the Marawi Compensation Board (MCB) is difficult. They even prioritize illegal claimants,” Madale said. “I hope our government …

author: rti_admin
title: The IITs: Tragic Failures That Beget More Tragedies
content:
From a social perspective, the IITs are tragic failures that beget more tragedies.

But you already know the IITs are the pinnacle of Indian aspirations, achievements, accolades, blah-di-blah, right? How about we celebrate by taking a closer look at the graduates, the faculty, and the institution?

The institutional charter, briefly. The IITs were conceived in 1946 to support the country’s industrial development and help meet the nation’s technological challenges. Parliament’s 1961 Act declares them institutions of national importance. It charges them with instruction and research, and with the advancement of learning and dissemination of knowledge. The same Act says every institute shall be open to persons of either sex and of whatever race, creed, caste or class, in admitting or appointing students and teachers alike. [1] Later laws reserve seats for SC, ST and OBC students, PhD seats included, and, since 2019, teaching posts at every rank.

Start with the product. As any IIT alum would confirm, a majority of IIT graduates wouldn’t be able to properly describe what ‘engineering’ is. Poorly educated and narrowly conditioned to chase status from a young age, most of them used to end up in finance or as middle management in US IT firms, but have lately diversified into mercenary ouroboros via IIT coaching and YouTube influencing. The institute’s own numbers: in IIT Bombay’s placement report for 2023–24, 29% of offers were in engineering and technology. The rest went to IT, consulting, finance, analytics and “other”. [2]

The defence is usually the famous founders. Let’s do the math. Seats went from about 2k a year in the 80s to about 20k now, so total grads ~400k. Unicorn founders ~117, high value startup founders maybe four thousand if you’re generous. So, 0.03% and 1%. [3, 4] Like unicorns, these founders are statistical anomalies. Sensible folks within the system will themselves readily acknowledge that their success is mostly despite it rather than because of it. And given the stated mission, funnelling billions in public subsidy into private equity accumulation for a minuscule minority is cause for shame rather than something to tom-tom about.

This is the deal then. Ruin your childhood to join an exclusive band of svayambhu achievers. Concoct jagatguru-brand gig economy “innovations” for exploiting cheap labor. Garland each other for contributions to the economic miracle of jobless growth and extractive digital feudalism. Parade your arrogant indifference or offer defensive apologies for the mockery of a social contract, dressed up in a lazy pragmatism argument about success.

By the way, who’s even there to teach them? Across all 23 IITs, 4,804 of 12,498 sanctioned teaching posts stood vacant in January 2026, or 38.4%. [5] It was 38.3% in December 2022. [6] In the nine IITs that disclosed the breakdown, about 60% of the empty posts were reserved ones. [5] Cryogenic sthiratva.

Sour grapes? I was there, eating them for four lost years. So chill. First week in the hostel, the rank was a common icebreaker question you asked people along with where they were from and in what department. Some hesitant answers made me stop asking. Only the rare, confident stud would openly declare he was SC, came through the preparatory course etc. The term in use was ‘schaddu’, and people would murmur in the early semesters, but soon some of them were ahead on GPA, and the murmurs lost voice. Years later, a friend who got a PhD mentioned feeling conflicted using reservations since their father was also a PhD and they went to good schools. Not long ago, an alum stated that even though they got in via reservation, everything after was earned by merit. I couldn’t make out if this was being defensive or proud. I don’t remember hearing of any campus suicides, and only learned about them from ‘The Death of Merit’ documentary. [7]

A decade after graduation and on another continent, the sourness still stung, in an interview by another pitiable alum. I was struggling for purpose and careening across career lanes. Unusual for an IIT grad, and he got suspicious… maybe I was a ‘category candidate’? author: chuang
title: “Every War Is a World War”: Interview with a Member of Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine
content:
The following is an interview with friends from Taiwan who have formed the umbrella coalition Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP). The interview includes an overview of the rifts in the Taiwanese left, and the frustration of TWAFP organizers carving out their place amid divisions between pro-unification and independence, or pro- and anti-American positions, in the contentious and highly polarized politics on the island.


The organizer recounts their efforts to confront Taiwan’s growing ties with Israel and direct support for the genocide in Palestine. They speak with sadness that, even as Taiwan is now the fourth-largest supplier of arms to Israel, surpassing mainland China, most Taiwanese care little for the distant genocide and the struggle in Palestine seems far away. And yet, TWAFP has led successful demonstrations, pulled together a broad coalition of disparate groups in support of Palestine, and conducted research to expose Taiwan’s complicity in the ongoing genocide.


Be sure to read their

report


from 2025, outlining specific pathways of material component support for Israel, including radar, armor, and an array of military hardware.


See also a recent

piece

 submitted to us, outlining Taiwan’s deepening ties with Israel under the DPP government.


–

Chuang


Q: To begin, let’s just set the stage. Over the last few years, the Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP) has helped to organize the largest mobilizations against the genocide in Palestine seen in Taiwan. Can you tell us a little about how TWAFP formed and maybe review some of the protests it has organized?


A:

Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP)

 was founded in April of 2024. Prior to this, Taiwan had already seen several groups doing Palestine advocacy work arise spontaneously, including Palestine Action Front, Taiwan Palestine Solidarity Network, and Parallel Government. As its name suggests, TWAFP is an “Alliance” that brings together groups that were already involved in initiatives related to Palestine. In addition to the three groups already mentioned, the alliance also includes a migrant worker organization, the

Taiwan International Workers’ Association (TIWA)

; the human rights organization, Taiwan Association for Human Rights; the cultural collective, Taiwan Rave & Punk Solidarity Front for Palestine; the gender issues group, Queer Margins; and the Christian group, Taiwan Olive Branch Peace Collective. From 2024 to today, we have organized one petitioning campaign, issued two open letters, held one candlelight vigil, hosted one book club meeting, staged five protest actions, held three press conferences, and organized three marches. In the future, we plan to engage in a number of other activities, many of which may be smaller in scale.


Q: TWAFP also did some very interesting research on material links between Taiwan and Israel. We can link to the report here, but can you briefly go over the main findings, and maybe go over any new information that you’ve found since that report was released? For example, have there been more details since then?

      


A: In September of 2025, we released our report,

Taiwanese Companies’ Complicity in Israel’s Ongoing Genocide

, which identified specific manufacturers assisting Israel in the production of military weapons, including via the production of components. For example: Gloria Material Technology Corp (GMTC) supplies superalloys and high-grade steel produced through electroslag remelting, while ADLINK Technology supplies embedded computing systems and industrial-grade computers. In another case, Transcom marketed its vertically integrated capabilities—spanning chip design to module production—to enter the Israeli defense supply chain and is now a key, long-term supplier of components for the EL/M-2084 multi-mission radar, which is a core element of the Israeli “Iron Dome” air defense system designed by Israeli defense company Elta.


Since the primary purpose of this report was to provide accurate information that could be used by media outlets and other organizations, who would ideally follow up with their own reporting and investigation, we were relatively restrained in our writing approach and did not engage in much interpretation or extrapolation. However, when I was conducting this research, I came across a number of findings that I want to share widely:

author: Unknown
title: Ulus: Healthcare must be free and accessible to all
content:
Structural problems in public hospitals and shortcomings in healthcare services are making it increasingly difficult for citizens to access medical care. People struggling to secure appointments through the Central Physician Appointment System (MHRS) sometimes have to wait at least 15 days just to submit an appointment request. Patients who eventually manage to obtain appointments after considerable effort must then try to explain their health problems within limited consultation times due to overcrowding in hospitals.


Difficulties in securing appointments and restrictions on consultation times are further deepening problems concerning the quality and accessibility of healthcare services.


Mehmet Nuri Ulus, Co-Chair of the Diyarbakır (Amed) Branch of the Health and Social Service Workers’ Union (SES), spoke to ANF about the problems facing public hospitals.


‘Healthcare is not being transformed, it is going backwards’


Ulus recalled that the Justice and Development Party (AKP) government has introduced healthcare reform and transformation programmes since 2002. He said that the policies implemented in recent years have caused serious problems in healthcare services and continued: “The AKP government has announced numerous programmes under the names of healthcare reform and healthcare transformation. However, particularly over the past 10 to 15 years, what has been called healthcare transformation has, from our perspective, meant collapse and regression. We have experienced both the COVID-19 pandemic and the earthquake during this period. These major crises showed us just how inadequate the healthcare system was in responding to the problems that arose.


The healthcare system should have been prepared for these crises and should have had the capacity to meet society's healthcare needs. Healthcare is a service that must be provided within the framework of the social welfare state. Everyone must be able to receive healthcare services equally, accessibly and in their mother tongue.


However, in recent years, we have seen healthcare services increasingly turn into a system in which those who have money can access care more easily. The proliferation of private hospitals is one aspect of this. Another is the emergence of an approach in which even public hospitals link faster access to certain tests, radiological examinations, medical reports and surgical procedures to payment. This undermines the principle that healthcare services should be equal for everyone.”


‘Physical queues have been replaced by virtual queues’


Ulus addressed the appointment crisis in the healthcare system, pointing out that the queues once seen outside hospitals now continue through the Central Physician Appointment System. He said appointment systems should make healthcare more accessible, but many citizens are currently unable to secure appointments.


Ulus said: “The AKP government used to say that people had to go to hospitals early in the morning and wait in queues to see a doctor. Today, physical queues have been replaced by virtual queues. Instead of waiting for hours outside hospitals, people now try to book appointments on their phones or online. However, when you access the system, you cannot find an available appointment. The queues have therefore not disappeared; they have simply changed form. Citizens now find themselves waiting in front of digital systems to access healthcare.


People face serious difficulties securing appointments, particularly in departments such as ear, nose and throat, ophthalmology and dermatology. Citizens who cannot obtain appointments are then forced to turn to private hospitals. However, considering the economic crisis, the struggle to make ends meet and the housing problems in Turkey, not everyone has the financial means to seek treatment at private hospitals.


As a result, the inability to access healthcare has become another dimension of economic hardship. Healthcare should be free and accessible, yet citizens are forced to stretch their financial resources to obtain the medical care they need.”


‘The budget is not allocated to preventive healthcare services’


Ulus said that the problems facing the healthcare system are not limited to difficulties in securing appointments. He drew attention to the following issues: “When we look at the Ministry of Health's budget and healthcare policies, we see that preventive healthcare services are consistently pushed into the background. Yet healthcare is …

author: Girard Mariano Lopez
title: Taipei Grand Mosque Board Faces Eviction Threat, Sparking Protests
content:
A DISPUTE OVER control of the Taipei Grand Mosque has spilled into protest after court enforcement against its board’s bank funds—raising concerns about donations, charitable services, and management of the historic religious site.

Dozens of Muslims from more than 10 countries gathered outside the Chinese Muslim Association’s office on October 16th. Organizers said demonstrations would continue every Friday after prayers until association leaders publicly addressed their concerns.

Yaser Cheng, chairman of the Taipei Grand Mosque Foundation, said the dispute threatened resources supporting a congregation that includes migrant workers and international students.

“They took the money from us,” Cheng said in an interview, describing funds he said included small donations from Indonesian workers and other worshippers. “It’s not from our board pocket.”

The Chinese Muslim Association, or CMA, has yet to respond to requests for an interview.

The conflict centers on competing claims over property rights and the authority to manage the mosque, which opened in 1960 and became a Taipei municipal historic monument in 1999. It remains a place of worship and a gathering point for Taiwan’s international Muslim community.

Cheng said the foundation had managed the mosque continuously for 66 years and should retain responsibility for its operations. He argued that its longstanding work gave it experience essential to maintaining religious services and community activities.

An analysis of court and banking documents supplied by Cheng supports a court-enforced collection of NT2,835,977 dollars from the foundation’s funds on September 24th, including a NT250 dollar fee. The bank transactions reconcile with the amount authorized in a Sept. 17 court order.

Cheng described the financial demands as rent and interest, saying the charging of interest was upsetting to worshippers because of Islam’s prohibition on riba (interest).

The documents, however, do not provide an itemized breakdown establishing how much of the collection represented rent, judgment interest, or other charges.

The mosque’s board put the broader financial impact at NT9.4 million dollars, including NT6.5 million that it said was frozen. Cheng explained that although the bank note does not reflect the freeze, they still cannot use it nor do they know how much more the CMA will take from the amount.

Records also list NT$7.5 million in remaining fixed deposits as of Oct. 1, but do not establish whether all those funds were accessible.

Cheng said financial pressure had curtailed assistance for poor people and plans to purchase cemetery land. However, he said the foundation would retain its employees despite the strain, describing its staffing resources as already limited.

He also accused the opposing institution of using financial pressure to force the board out. The documents establish that funds were collected through court enforcement but do not independently establish that motive or wrongdoing by either institution.

The documents include a September 2023 order requiring the foundation to vacate and return the mosque building. They do not establish that an eviction occurred or clarify the present status of proceedings concerning possession.

The property dispute stems partly from arrangements involving former landowner Chia Hsin Cement and the city’s efforts to preserve the mosque.

Cheng alleges that former mosque chairman Ma Chao-yen arranged for property rights to benefit the opposing foundation without proper board authorization.

But TaiSounds reported in January that prosecutors declined to indict Ma for breach of trust, finding insufficient grounds for prosecution over the arrangements. That decision did not resolve every separate civil or governance issue.

In earlier reporting by Taiwan’s Central News Agency’s Indonesian service, an unnamed representative of the opposing foundation said worship would continue and characterized disputed payments as tax-related.

For worshippers, uncertainty extends beyond the courtroom.

Raja Ramadhana, an Indonesian doctoral student at National Taiwan University of Science and Technology, said the dispute complicated his understanding of whom to approach when organizing community activities.

He said he usually worked with the mosque foundation but wanted the association to explain its position before drawing conclusions.

“For now, the information is so imbalanced,” Ramadhana said.

author: Sarah Raymundo
title: On liberal opportunism and the “purity” smear
content:
Photo from Naga City Tourism Facebook page

Accusing leftists and activists of demanding a “useless politics of purity” is a classic liberal defense mechanism designed to shift the burden of moral failure onto the critic.

Why did former Vice President and now Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo roll out the pink carpet for the Zionist war machine? When Robredo hosted Israeli Ambassador Dana Kursh for an official courtesy visit, she was not merely performing the routine gestures of local hospitality. She was actively welcoming and legitimizing representatives of the US-Israeli genocidal apparatus. This intervention centers an anti-imperialist analysis to dismantle the liberal apologetics surrounding this act. Rather than an isolated error in judgment, this diplomatic encounter exposes the persistent, foundational tension within the Philippine political landscape: the contradiction between liberal reformism and anti-imperialist national liberation.

Dismissing progressives’ critique of Robredo’s hosting of the Israeli envoy as mere “political purism” is politically and morally impoverished. The underlying mechanism demands a total, systematic critique. To understand why her defenders deploy the “politics of purity” accusation, and why that defense completely falls apart when examining real power dynamics and economic interests, we must lay bare both the liberal class position and the ideological sleight of hand at work.

To make sense of Robredo’s pivot toward imperial hospitality, we must look directly at the liberal class position. Her stance is neither an accidental misstep nor a personal failure of political intelligence but the direct expression of her class character and political alignment. Liberal reformism in the global periphery operates strictly within the legal, institutional, and geopolitical framework dictated by US imperialism.

While Robredo served as a focal point against the overt state terrorism of the Marcos-Duterte dynasties, her opposition was strictly intra-class—a feud over how to manage the neocolonial state, pitting rule-of-law decorum against autocratic violence.

Because her political legitimacy rests upon acceptance by the global capitalist order, her opposition stops at the border of imperial interest. When forced to choose between international solidarity with an anti-imperialist national liberation movement and alignment with the Washington-Tel Aviv axis, liberal reformists invariably side with the imperial core. They cannot critique the drain of value, the extraction of labor, or the military hegemony of US imperialism because their entire political project depends on remaining within that very apparatus.

This structural subservience explains why defenders deploy the “purity politics” weapon whenever that alignment is exposed. Accusing leftists and activists of demanding a “useless politics of purity” is a classic liberal defense mechanism designed to shift the burden of moral failure onto the critic. From a materialist standpoint, this argument relies on three ideological fallacies:

First, it replaces a materialist baseline with ideological absolution. Opposition to active genocide, ethnic cleansing, and imperialist aggression is not a performative or elevated ideological standard; it is the absolute baseline of human solidarity and anti-imperialist struggle. Labeling principled opposition to mass slaughter as “purity” redefines baseline morality as an unreasonable demand, attempting to pass off complicity as pragmatic maturity.

Second, it operates on the logic of liberal idealism, which treats political stances as abstract moral choices made in a vacuum. Political actions reflect concrete class interests. Shielding a public figure from accountability for legitimizing a settler-colonial state serves a specific political function: it conditions the middle forces to accept imperial violence as a routine, acceptable feature of global diplomacy.

Third, it trades scientific alignment for unprincipled unity. Transformative praxis distinguishes between principled unity—built on anti-imperialist struggle and mass interest—and unprincipled unity, which colludes with reaction to preserve electoral coalitions. Demanding that the progressive movement remain silent on international solidarity to protect a liberal politician’s image trades human rights and anti-imperialist consciousness for temporary electoral expediency.

This dynamic reveals the distinct role of the middle forces—segments of the …

author: Luca Tavan
title: Europe’s youth and workers in revolt
content:
The metaphor of a tinderbox is one of the most overused in politics. But how else could you describe the situation in Europe today, where every small spark of resistance seems to be catching and turning into a powerful blaze? 

Things kicked off in France in late September, when students in the working-class suburb of Créteil in the South-east of Paris blockaded their school in protest against poor conditions. This has since grown into the deepest challenge French President Emmanuel Macron has faced in his ten years in power. On October 17, students were joined by workers in a national mobilisation of 800,000. Strikes, demonstrations, blockades and riots have all played a role in this movement. It’s not just the radical left comparing this situation to the legendary student and worker uprising of May 1968.

In Spain, anger at the eviction of María del Carmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman whose rent was raised 230 percent when her apartment was acquired by an investment firm, has generated a massive movement for housing justice. The streets have forced the centre-left Sanchez government to call early elections, and typically hesitant union leaders to schedule a general strike for November 11. 

Protests have rocked Albania since May, in response to an environmentally catastrophic luxury resort development tied to the Trump family. On October 13, youth inspired by the French protests brought their own demands over education and wages into the mix, turning the movement into a national uprising. Government buildings have been invaded and burnt, and the call for the downfall of Edi Rama’s government is widespread. It is the country’s largest revolt since the fall of Stalinist regime in the early 1990s.  

In Italy, mass protests pledging to “fare come in Francia” (to do as in France) last weekend turned into standoffs against the police. In Milan, 250 people were detained, more than 80 percent of whom were minors. Belgium, Portugal, and Ireland have seen mass protests and strikes taking aim at austerity and intolerable working conditions. 

This marks the biggest wave of protests on the continent in at least a generation. Anyone who wants to see capitalism one day toppled and replaced with a system really fit for human beings should take great hope from these events. 

There’s no telling how long these struggles will continue, whether they will lose momentum, or if massive state repression will succeed in intimidating many off the streets. But this convergence of different struggles provides a glimpse of the possibility of rebuilding class-based politics after a decade characterised by despair and far right ascendancy. 

The roots of the revolt 

While these different movements are profoundly shaped by their specific national contexts, they have common roots in decades of battered living standards and attacks on workers. An entire generation suffered the consequences of the 2008 economic crisis - wages were slashed, young people were left without the prospect of ever finding a job, and social services were gutted to bail out the banks. 

Italy provides perhaps the sharpest example of the consequences of this class war waged by the rich: according to data from Italy's Parliamentary Budget Office, private sector workers have seen their real wages fall by 6.6 percent between 1990 and 2026. 

In countries experiencing economic recovery, young people are learning that they bear the costs of boom as well as bust. New jobs created are insecure, and wage increases are offset by soaring housing costs. 

This long, bitter experience has brought questions of social class back to the fore and changed the character of struggle. A comparison of the current occupation of Madrid’s Puerta del Sol with the last one is instructive. 2011’s 

Indignados

movement shared many characteristics with the protests of today, fuelled by anger at low wages, evictions and the callousness of the political class. It was an inspiring and important moment for the left. But the politics of the movement were organically populist, seeking to build a cross-class alliance of Spanish ‘citizens’ against the political caste they blamed for the country’s ruin. The most popular slogans reflected this - like “real democracy now!” and “they don’t represent us”. 

This sentiment was also expressed in a hostility to the organised left and workers’ movement within the occupation - seen by many participants as just another facet of the “politics” they felt alienated from …

author: Pip Hinman
title: NSW Labor to introduce law overriding High Court coal mine ruling
content:
The NSW Labor government will introduce a law to allow MACH Energy to expand output at its contested Mount Pleasant coal mine in the Upper Hunter region of NSW, in response to a High Court ruling that invalidated the expansion approval.

The High Court ruled on October 7 that the NSW Independent Planning Commission (IPC) failed to consider how pollution from its coal would affect the region. It also emphasised that the IPC must consider Scope 3 — downstream emissions from coal burned elsewhere, including overseas — as part of its approval process.

Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (DAMSHEG) first challenged the IPC’s approval in 2023 in the NSW Land and Environment Court. Following a protracted legal battle, DAMSHEG had its case upheld in the High Court.

Premier Chris Minns told the ABC on October 19 that he was moving to protect jobs that would be “on the line”. He said the new law would “guarantee” 400 direct jobs until 2032 — the deadline for the temporary extension MACH Energy sought and was given, even though the High Court was considering MACH Energy’s case against DAMSHEG.

The mining corporation wants a licence to mine thermal coal until 2048 — something Minns and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese support.

However, the 22-year extension of the coal mine would include no guarantee of 400 jobs. DAMSHEG’s Tony Lonergan said the mine relies on contractors who can be laid off at any time.

Wendy Wales, also from DAMSHEG, said she wants fossil fuel workers to be able to transition to alternative employment. “We have never wanted anyone in the Hunter to lose their livelihood.”

“A law written for one company, days after the High Court ruled against that company, is an inappropriate use of the NSW legislative process,” she said. “The laws should reflect a balance where the overall welfare of citizens and environment is paramount and industry serves the needs of all citizens.”

The NSW Minerals Council welcomed Labor’s move. Chief executive Stephen Galilee said: “The Mount Pleasant mine has endured four years of activist legal challenges, creating uncertainty for hundreds of mine workers, their families and local supplier businesses.”

Greens MLC Sue Higginson said NSW Labor is being “fed lies about the job numbers at Mount Pleasant” and “selling the integrity of the NSW planning and legal systems down the river”.

She said MACH Energy had threatened to sack 400 workers at Mount Pleasant mine unless Labor introduced this law. It has been revealed that new job advertisements were posted by MACH Energy shortly after Minns announced the special law allowing expanded coal mining.

“MACH Energy’s own documents show that the increased coal mining that will be allowed by Minns’ special laws would only create around 100 jobs, completely undermining its threat to fire 400 workers if they didn’t get their way,” Higginson said.

“This is state capture — a form of modern day corruption ... where billion dollar corporations are writing laws that benefit them, in defiance of the law as laid down by the High Court of Australia.”

Retired Supreme Court judge Anthony Whealy has called for an independent review of the Minns government’s decision to draft laws to circumvent the High Court ruling.

Whealy told the ABC on October 20 that the government’s decision is “reprehensible” because it “obliterates” the legal process.

“The idea that a substantial mining venture can approach the government and say, ‘Look, let’s go behind the court processes and sort this out between ourselves’ is a very dangerous precedent, and that’s exactly what appears to have happened here,” Whealy said.

“They’ve effectively ignored what I would call respect for the rule of law by overriding it.”

The Greens are supporting his call for an independent review.

Higginson said Labor has “decided to step over the independent planning process ... the High Court of Australia and they are trashing the rule of law”.

The ABC also reported on October 20 that MACH Energy is being investigated over allegations it breached its coal production limits, as it scaled up construction during the High Court appeal process.

Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group

author: Dougal McNeill
title: Striking for Palestine in Aotearoa
content:
Thousands of workers at universities and polytechnics (TAFEs) across Aotearoa (New Zealand) went on strike Wednesday 21 October, rallying against poor pay offers and the increasing precarity of employment in tertiary education. This was exciting enough on its own terms. The last time we went on strike, in 2022, it was the first in decades, and felt like something new. Now tertiary workers join teachers, public servants, health workers and others who have taken action over the last two years.

Our right-wing coalition government has attacked many of our rights but, in the fightback against their assault on everything from Te Tiriti o Waitangi (the country’s founding treaty with Indigenous groups) to pay equity, we’ve seen that the long drought around industrial action in these islands has been broken by welcome and nourishing rain.

Each bargaining campaign has different priorities and, at Te Herenga Waka in Wellington, my university, one part of our campaign stands out. We went on strike for Palestine. University Workers for Palestine, a campaign group bringing together staff across the country, emerged from the anti-genocide protests since 2023 to make concrete demands of institutions here. One focus is university superannuation schemes and their investments, including in weapons companies and others connected to Israel’s ongoing war against the Palestinians. A core part of our demands, then, is for the superannuation scheme to divest from the genocide.

We are striking for the “Three Ps”: pay, precarity and Palestine. The last of those got the loudest cheers at the strike rally yesterday, and there were signs from “Librarians for Palestine” to staff committing “from the river to the sea” that Palestine will be free. Unionised workers here have shown that our action for everyday pay and conditions can be linked to a wider vision of justice and liberation.

It’s a small start, but an exciting one, and another sign that the protest moment of 2023 has, over the years, become a long-term movement for Palestinian freedom.

author: Kerry Smith
title: Hunter Jobs Alliance says new law on coal transition gives hope
content:
The Future Jobs and Investment Authority (FJIA) Bill 2025 passed both NSW houses on October 20.

According to the Hunter Jobs Alliance (HJA), it is a major achievement and testimony to the many organisations and individuals that have campaigned over five years to secure a better future for workers, communities and the environment across NSW’s four coal regions.

HJA started with publishing Building for the Future: A ‘Hunter Valley Authority’ to secure our region’s prosperity in June 2021, which made the case for a “dedicated regional authority to support workers, diversify our economy and secure the Hunter’s future beyond coal”.

Since then, it has worked to get NSW Labor to commit to establishing a Transition Authority in its policy platform before the March election next year.

It is seeking 10 amendments to strengthen the law, particularly workforce transition planning obligations for coal companies.

HJA singled out the Australian Manufacturing Workers’ Union for “critical political and strategic support in advancing the proposal”, as well as Hunter Renewal, which championed this reform long before HJA’s involvement.

It said the new law establishes a dedicated public authority, and funds to support economic diversification, attract new industries and create jobs across NSW’s four coal regions.

“Importantly, it will also require coal mine owners to develop workforce transition plans to support workers affected by mine closures. This represents a significant shift from the current system, where coal companies have had limited enforceable responsibilities to prepare workers and communities for closure.”

HJA said its next job is to ensure the regulations are “developed and finalised before the caretaker period” in the lead-up to the March election next year.

“These must establish meaningful minimum standards for workforce transition plans, including paid retraining, paid training leave, career and financial advice, and assistance securing new employment.”

HJA is also seeking at least $150 million each year for the Future Jobs and Investment Fund, up from the current $22.5 million a year. “Securing this as a budget commitment ahead of the March 2027 election will be a key focus.”

HJA said its member organisations and everyone who has contributed to this campaign “demonstrates what can be accomplished when unions, environmental organisations, community groups, business and industry work together towards a shared vision for the future of the Hunter and NSW’s other coal regions”.

Future Jobs and Investment Fund

author: Robert Narai
title: Hungary 1956: a workers’ revolution against Stalinism
content:
Seventy years ago, Hungarian workers and students rose up against a brutal dictatorship that justified itself in the language of Marxism. In its place, they built workers’ councils: organs of working-class democracy, giving future generations a chance to discover the essence of revolutionary Marxism.

My grandfather, Vendel Koroknai, often played Beethoven’s Egmont Overture on his record player and spoke fondly of its role in the 1956 revolution. The overture tells the story of Lamoral, count of Egmont, who defied Spanish tyranny under the duke of Alba. His execution sparked a broader rebellion that led to Dutch independence. For the Hungarians who heard it, the parallels were striking: the Russians as the oppressive occupiers, themselves as the Dutch seeking self-determination.

They heard it because on the evening of 23 October 1956, workers and students defeated the hated AVH, the secret police of the dictatorship that had ruled Hungary for the previous eight years, in fierce street fighting and gun battles, and took control of Magyar Radio in central Budapest. They turned it into a hub for broadcasting news, appeals, morale-boosting content and, importantly, political arguments about the way forward for their revolution. Between announcements, they played the overture over and over to lift people’s spirits and give them the resolve to fight a much better-armed enemy in the form of Russian tanks. It became the unofficial anthem of the revolution. My grandfather, who at the time was a farm labourer on the outskirts of Debrecen (Hungary’s second-largest city) and a delegate and militia leader in one of the workers’ councils, recalled: “It wasn’t just filler. It was a prophecy, articulating the hopes, dreams and aspirations of a people fighting for their liberation.”

Whether they knew it or not, Hungarian workers and students were also creating a radical alternative to both Stalinist and Western barbarism. At the height of the Cold War, they broke the so-called communist regime’s repressive arms—the secret police were dispersed, the police defected or stood aside, the army disintegrated—even as parts of its executive and bureaucratic machinery kept functioning. Into the space that opened up, they built workers’ councils, elected and recallable, running factories, farms, whole cities and towns. My grandfather was one of those workers, and it was his first taste of any political freedoms.

Stalinists who defend the bureaucratic monstrosities of the Soviet Union have always called this a counter-revolution, the work of fascists and Western agents, and used that claim to justify sending in the tanks. (The term “tankie” is derived from this argument.) The Hungarian far right, Viktor Orbán chief among them, calls it something else: a rehearsal for 1989 and the fall of the “communist” system, proto-capitalists fighting to restore private property and the free market. Neither is true. Hungarian workers were not fighting for capitalism, Stalinist or Western. The councils they built were organs of workers’ power and the basis for a democratic society run by the working class: genuine socialism and communism. This was a workers’ revolution, and the people who made it included men like my grandfather, who had lost his family’s farm to the regime that now called him a fascist.

As the American Trotskyist Hal Draper wrote at the time: “Hungary opens a new era with the first revolution against the Stalinist system.” Hungarian workers and students proved the working class could still make revolutions. They proved the so-called communist regimes were counterrevolutionary. And they cracked, for the first time on this scale, the grip Stalinism held over communist parties across the world.


PART ONE: THE OCTOBER UPRISING

Background

The Red Army occupied Hungary at the end of World War Two. With the tacit approval of the West, a Russian-backed dictatorship was installed under Mátyás Rákosi, who called himself “Stalin’s best Hungarian disciple”. Like the other Eastern European regimes established at this time, Hungary called itself a “workers’ state”. It was anything but. Workers like my grandfather had to perform backbreaking labour to meet production targets set by bureaucrats. They had no say in what was produced or how, or in any broader political decision. They were paid pitiful wages that could hardly buy bread and milk.

Peasants were driven into collective farms at gunpoint, and the hatred this produced never went away. (My …

author: Sue Bolton
title: Sue Bolton: ‘Put working-class communities first’
content:
Sue Bolton, a fourth-term Socialist Alliance councillor at the Merri-bek City Council, is running for Broadmeadows in the Victorian elections.

This article is based on a speech she gave to the launch of SA’s campaign. The party is fielding candidates in Broadmeadows and Pascoe Vale in Naarm/Melbourne, and in four seats covering Djilang/Geelong. It is also standing in the Northern Metropolitan and Western Region for the Legislative Council.

Socialist Alliance’s campaign slogan “Fighting for people, not the billionaires” encapsulates our view that fundamental change won’t come from elected representatives.

Our approach is to work with communities getting organised so that they can become really strong. We need members of parliament who will champion a politics that defends working-class communities against the billionaires.

The only way to guarantee that working-class communities’ rights are safeguarded is by electing socialists who are also committed community activists.

The campaign to stop the redevelopment of the toxic site in Fawkner in 2017 is a case in point. When this development came through Merri-bek City Council, I objected and together with the community we fought hard against it. It would have sailed through because the Environmental Protection Authority had already approved it.

Right now the far right — and the mainstream right — are trying to take back social and political rights that took fights to win.

The Victorian Labor Party, following the One Nation (ON) playbook, is attacking migrants. It has stopped talking about renewable energy and the need to transition away from fossil fuels. Even if ON doesn’t get an MP, its policy announcements are pushing the major parties to the right — a core part of the billionaires’ divide-and-rule plan.

Billionaire mining magnate Gina Rinehart is writing Pauline Hanson’s policies. She has other billionaire supporters, but they prefer to remain in the shadows.

If migration was to be stopped tomorrow, there would still be a housing crisis. This is because state and federal policies allow developers and speculators to game the system. The destruction of public housing is another part of the housing problem.

What is the billionaire’s agenda? Pay zero or little tax and privatise, or cut, public services — not the fat cats but the people providing the services.

Even repairing potholes on roads and motorways has become political, after a man tragically died after hitting a pothole on his motorbike. VicRoads used to do those repairs. Since it has been handed to the private sector, the roads have deteriorated.

Labor’s privatisation agenda of critical public assets includes the Port of Melbourne, part of VicRoads and the Land Titles office. It includes demolishing 44 high-rise public housing towers, shafting people out of their communities and affordable homes.

The disintegration of the community health sector is part of this. The introduction of the national disability insurance scheme (NDIS) forced the community health centres to move to a user-pays model.

But communities have also shown that they will resist. Because of the community revolt, Labor’s plan to axe GPs and other services at various CoHealth sites, including Collingwood and Fitzroy, have been saved — for the moment.

While Premier Ben Carroll has sought to distance himself from Jacinta Allan and Dan Andrews, he supports the public housing demolition. Labor should be pledging to renovate and keep the public housing towers, and replace the dwellings that have been demolished.

The billionaire class wants to stop workers gaining pay rises which keep up with inflation. It wants to remove regulations so private businesses, like the mega data centre AI industry, or developers eyeing off the toxic site in Fawkner, can do whatever they like.

It is possible after the next election that the Treaty process in Victoria could be ripped up. The Coalition has promised to do that and ON would like to. Sections of Labor are nervous about the kind of rights First Nations people would have with a Treaty or treaties.

For First Nations people, the process is about more than symbolism; it is a way of improving their lives, including access to culture and practice to build stronger communities. This is important. We need to ensure that the rights of First Nations people are enhanced. Only then will we have improved rights for everybody.

author: Tom Bramble
title: US imperialism in the 21st century
content:
At the start of this century, US imperialism was at its peak. It had been a decade since its chief adversary, the Soviet Union, had crumbled; the country was now the unchallenged global superpower. Washington was bringing countries into the North Atlantic Treaty Organization that had been the USSR’s satellites in Europe, and it could rely on its allies to extend US influence into every corner of the world.

The US dominated the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund and was the most powerful nation in the United Nations. Its economy was booming, and the federal government ran surpluses. US multinationals found new markets and investment outlets worldwide. It was the heyday of “globalisation”. The US ruling class boasted that the country was a beacon to the world. As Democratic candidate Al Gore put it in one of the presidential debates in 2000:

“It is a great tribute to our founders that 224 years later this nation is now looked to by the peoples on every other continent and the peoples from every part of this Earth as a kind of model for what their future could be … The power of example is America’s greatest power in the world.”

Twenty-five years later, US rulers are not so assured. The country has suffered a series of crises, and the global balance of power has shifted. The US remains the world’s leading power, but it is wracked by dysfunction on a series of fronts. Its allies are increasingly estranged. Wars in the Middle East have exposed its diminished military power. Its tech sector and banks still lead, but its industrial base is now much weaker. Its political system is seen not as a model for what to do, but what to avoid. 

The decay of US power can be understood as the result of four interrelated phenomena: an imperial crisis in the Middle East, an economic crisis that crashed the world, the challenge from China and a political crisis that reflects and exacerbates these three trends.

The imperial crisis

The 9/11 attack on the World Trade Center in 2001 was a devastating blow to America’s sense of invulnerability. But US strategists also recognised the attack as an opportunity to advance US power—justification for a new round of wars that would intimidate the country’s rivals and allies alike and overcome the Vietnam-era legacy of widespread domestic opposition to far-flung and lengthy land wars. 

The idea of an aggressive revival of US military interventionism had been germinating in the ranks of the Republican Party for some years in its “neoconservative” wing. The leading think tank was the Project for a New American Century, founded by William Kristol and Robert Kagan. Its supporters and associates included Dick Cheney, Donald Rumsfeld, Paul Wolfowitz and John Bolton, all of whom held senior positions in the George W. Bush administration, which had won the 2000 election. 

The October 2001 invasion of Afghanistan was the first step in this wider project. Bush’s cabinet believed that the US would topple the ruling Taliban in Kabul and then lead a triumphal march through the capitals of its defeated enemies. Iraq, Iran and Syria were the main targets and, further afield, North Korea. Regime change was the objective.

In the short term, the invasion of Afghanistan was a stunning success. The Taliban were overthrown within two months. Domestic support for the war was overwhelming. It seemed US imperialism was back. Next was Iraq. The Bush administration justified its invasion by associating the country’s president, Saddam Hussein, with the 9/11 attacks and claiming that he had built an arsenal of weapons of mass destruction to threaten the West. On 19 March 2003, the US and its allies invaded Iraq. Within three weeks, US forces had taken Baghdad, and on 1 May Bush appeared on the deck of the

USS Abraham Lincoln

 to declare “mission accomplished”. 

Yet things turned bad for the US in both countries. In Iraq, local resistance to the occupation soon emerged. By the following year, it was raging. The US responded by flattening whole neighbourhoods, deploying white phosphorus and uranium-tipped weapons. Regular sweeps of suspected resistance activists terrified neighbourhoods and filled the jails. The US destroyed civilian infrastructure providing clean water, power and health care. And it sacked more than 100,000 government employees, creating mass unemployment and impoverishing millions. The death toll rose steadily. A study by the

Lancet

 journal in 2006 estimated 655,000 excess deaths in …

author: Jim McIlroy
title: The giant ‘swiftie’ begs for an end to coal
content:
More than 50 people joined the protest which was organised by Lock the Gate Alliance (LGA).

The swift parrot, which won the Bird of the Year prize in 2023, has been described as the world’s fastest parrot.

Nick Clyde from LGA told the rally that the swift parrot was being endangered by NSW Labor's approvals of new coal and gas projects. “There are currently 17 coal mine expansion projects in the pipeline in NSW.”

Raymond “Bubbly” Weatherall, an Gomeroi man, said: “State and federal governments have approved every coal and gas project that they can. Enough is enough! The end game is to get coal and gas out of our country.”

Doro Babeck, NSW campaigner for the Bob Brown Foundation, said the campaign to save the swift parrot and other species focused on protecting the native forests in Tasmania and elsewhere. “The swift parrot flies from Tasmania across Bass Strait to the mainland in three hours. That trip takes up to 12 hours by boat.”

Sally Hunter, an anti-coal mine campaigner and a Maules Creek farmer, asked people to send a message to the government to let the Maules Creek mine lease lapse.

“We need a plan for the transition of mining jobs out of coal and gas and into renewable industries. The Maules Creek mine has already bought out around 80 farms in the area, and this has to stop.”

The model swift parrot, which was constructed in Muloobinba/Newcastle, will now be transported to Maules Creek for a gathering with the local community.

[For more information on the Swift Parrot campaign visit Lock the Gate Alliance.]
